SPF as a Daily Anchor, and the Quiet Reordering of a Modern Skincare Routine
A white sunscreen tube on a sunny bathroom shelf
Sunscreen is no longer about the beach. It is the single most considered step in a modern routine.

For most of the history of sunscreen as a product, it was sold as a thing you took on holiday. You bought it in May. You applied it generously on the first hot weekend of the year, when the sun came through the car windscreen and the back of your neck prickled. You reapplied it on the beach. You came home with a tan or a burn, depending on your luck, and the bottle sat on the bathroom shelf for the rest of the year, waiting for its next Mediterranean fortnight. This is no longer how most of us use sunscreen, and it is no longer how most of us should think about it.

The shift has happened quietly, and is now happening quickly. Sunscreen, in the last ten years, has moved from being a beach accessory to being the foundation of almost every thoughtful routine. Dermatologists, having spent decades trying to convince the public of this, finally have something close to consensus behind them. The sun is, by a comfortable margin, the single most important environmental factor in how a face looks at fifty. Not the cleanser we used, or the serum we could afford, or the night cream we forgot to put on half the nights of our twenties. The sun. Everything else, in the long accounting of a face, is a footnote.

![A white sunscreen tube on a sunny bathroom shelf](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1557704507-02fd6eb73fe3?crop=entropy&cs=tinysrgb&w=1800&q=82)

## Why the sun matters so much

The skin is the body's interface with the world, and the sun is the part of the world that does the most to it. Ultraviolet light, in particular, is what dermatologists spend most of their careers trying to protect us from. There are two kinds that matter. UVA is the longer wavelength, the one that penetrates deeper into the skin, the one that does most of the slow, cumulative damage we associate with aging - the brown patches, the fine lines, the slight leathery quality that a face takes on after decades of inadvertent exposure. UVB is the shorter wavelength, the one that burns, the one that is the direct cause of most skin cancers. A modern sunscreen protects against both, which is what the "broad spectrum" label is meant to convey.

The reason this matters, day to day, is that the sun we encounter in our normal lives is more than enough to do all of this damage. The myth that you only need sunscreen on bright days, or only when you are visibly hot, or only on holiday, is one of the more persistent pieces of misinformation in the beauty category. UV light comes through clouds. It comes through car windows. It comes through the windows of offices. It is reflected off water, off concrete, off snow. We are, on most days and in most cities, in, it turns out, significantly more sun than we think we are.

This is also why the question of SPF has, over the last decade, stopped being a beach question and started being a daily one. The sunscreen we apply on a Tuesday in February, walking to the train, matters just as much as the sunscreen we apply on a Saturday in July on a boat. Probably more, in fact, because we are more likely to forget it.

## What a number actually means

The SPF number on a bottle is one of the more misunderstood things in personal care, and it is worth pausing on. SPF stands for sun protection factor. It is a measure of how much longer, compared to wearing no sunscreen at all, you can be in the sun before you start to burn. An SPF of 30 means, in theory, that you can be out for thirty times longer than you could without it. An SPF of 50 means fifty times. The relationship, like, says - the key word being in theory - is not linear. The jump from 30 to 50 is a smaller jump than the jump from 5 to 25. By 50, you have most of the protection that any sunscreen can offer.

What this means, in practice, is that SPF 30, applied properly, is enough for most days. The high-protection SPFs - 70, 90, 100 - are mostly a marketing concession to the sense that more must be better. They offer marginally more protection. They often feel heavier on the face. For most of us, most of the time, SPF 30 is the right place to be. We should not, however, take the number on the bottle to mean we are protected for the length of a working day. The number assumes an application that most of us do not achieve. The honest way to think about sunscreen is not in terms of SPF at all but in terms of application.

The amount that actually delivers the SPF on the label is roughly a quarter teaspoon for the face. A quarter teaspoon is more than most of us use. It is the amount that takes a moment to rub in, that leaves a slight cast for a few minutes, that feels, for a few seconds, like too much. This is normal. This is what the right amount feels like. If the sunscreen disappears instantly into the skin, the way a serum does, we have probably used half of what we needed.

## The texture question

One of the most significant changes in the sunscreen category, in the last five years, has been the texture. The old sunscreens - the ones our parents used, the ones that were designed to be applied once a day on a beach towel - were thick. They were white. They had a particular smell that became, for an entire generation, the smell of sunscreen, although it had less to do with sunscreen than with the chemical filters of the era. They sat on the skin. They made the skin look, in photographs, slightly grey. They were, by modern standards, unpleasant to wear, which is part of the reason most of us did not wear them every day.

The modern sunscreen is a different object. The new chemical filters do not have the smell. The mineral filters have been micronized to the point where they do not leave a visible cast, at least in most of the better formulations. The textures, generally, are lighter. The best of them, the ones made by the brands that have spent serious money on formulation, feel like a moisturizer with a job. They are not invisible. They are not meant to be invisible. But they are wearable, in the way the older sunscreens were not, which is why so many of us are now applying them, every morning, regardless of whether we plan to leave the house.

This is, finally, the thing that has shifted the conversation. The technology caught up with the science. The dermatologists had been telling us, for decades, to wear sunscreen every day. We had not been doing it, because the products available had not been good enough to make the habit stick. The newer formulations, finally, are good enough. We are beginning to believe the science because the products have become a pleasure to use.

## The morning ritual

Where, then, does sunscreen go in the routine? This is one of the questions the beauty press has spent some time on, and the answer is simpler than it sounds. Sunscreen should be the last step of the morning routine, applied after moisturizer and before makeup. The reason for this is that sunscreen needs to sit on the surface to work. If we apply it and then apply anything on top, we are partly undoing the application. If we apply it on top of a moisturizer, the moisturizer is doing the moisturizing and the sunscreen is doing the sunblocking, and they are not interfering with each other.

For those of us who wear makeup, the question becomes more complex. Foundation with SPF is better than no sunscreen and worse than an actual sunscreen. The SPF in most foundations is achieved at a much lower concentration than the SPF in a sunscreen. It is a useful backup. It is not a substitute. The most reliable approach is to apply a dedicated sunscreen, give it a minute to settle, and then apply whatever we want on top.

For those of us who do not wear makeup, the question is simpler. Sunscreen, on its own, is a fine finish. The slightly dewy look that a well-formulated SPF leaves on the skin is, in most lights, more interesting than wearing nothing at all. It is also the most consequential thing we will do for our face all day.

## What daily use actually does

It is worth being honest, here, about what daily sunscreen can and cannot do. It cannot reverse damage that has already been done. It cannot, on its own, address the fine lines and the pigmentation changes that have already accumulated. It can, however, prevent most of the damage that would otherwise accumulate over the next twenty years. This is the actual arithmetic of it. We are not making our faces younger. We are keeping our faces where they are.

This is also why the question is no longer whether to wear it, but how to wear it in a way that does not feel like a chore. The texture matters. The packaging matters. The fact that we like the bottle, that we keep it on the bathroom shelf where we can see it, that we are not annoyed by the smell - all of this matters, because the product that stays on the shelf is the one that gets used. The product that gets used is the one that does the work.

There is a quiet pleasure, once the habit has been established, in reaching for the same bottle on most mornings of most weeks. It becomes one of the small fixed points around which the day organizes itself. We brush our teeth. We apply the SPF. We look, briefly, at ourselves in the mirror, in the kind of light that does not flatter anyone, and we leave the bathroom and we go. The sun is out there, as it always is, doing what it always does. We have made our small daily decision against it. That is, in the long run, what the face will remember.

Stargazing, and the Free Theater Above the Roofline
A night sky filled with stars above a dark horizon
Stepping outside at midnight, looking up, and finding the same constellations your grandmother saw — the only subscription that has not raised its price.

There is a moment, somewhere around midnight, when the house has finally gone quiet and the dog has finally stopped asking to be let out, and you are, for no particular reason, standing in the back garden, in your socks, looking up. The roofline of the house is in front of you, black against a slightly less black sky. A plane is crossing, very slowly, with its red light blinking. The wind has dropped. The neighbour's security lamp has, mercifully, gone off. And above all of this, very quietly, the stars are there. They have been there all evening. They have been there all your life. But you have not, in any practical sense, looked at them in months. And now, on a Tuesday in October, in your socks, in the back garden, you are looking at them. And they are, as they always have been, completely extraordinary.

We want to argue, gently, for the stars. Not in the grand way. Not in the astronomical way. We want to argue for the practice of stepping outside, at night, and looking up. We want to argue for it because it is, in our experience, the only entertainment that is still, after a long period of every other entertainment getting worse, completely free. The stars have not raised their price. The stars have not introduced a premium tier. The stars have not, as far as we know, begun selling advertising around the moon. The show is free. The show is the only show that has been free, on this particular patch of earth, since long before there was a show to charge for.

This is what we mean by free theater. The sky, above the roofline, is a theater. The theater has been running, every night, for several billion years. The theater does not require a ticket, although it does, like all good theaters, require the audience to turn up on time, which in this case means at night, in the dark, when the audience is, ideally, slightly underdressed for the occasion. The theater is the most generous cultural institution in your life, and you have, almost certainly, been ignoring it for years.

## what the dark does for you

The first thing the night sky does, when you step outside, is what the dark does to a body that has been indoors for too long. The dark quiets the body. The dark quiets, also, the small, busy apparatus of seeing — the screens, the lit rooms, the streetlamps, the small blinking lights on the kitchen counter that say, in their quiet way, that everything in the house is still connected to the internet. The dark turns off, gently and without asking, the part of you that has been processing input. The dark gives you back, in exchange, the eyes themselves.

This is what we have lost, in the modern city. The dark, in any useful quantity, has become hard to find. We have, with the best of intentions, lit the night. We have lit it with streetlamps, with porch lights, with security floods, with the small blinking diodes on every device. We have made the night, in most of our neighbourhoods, an extension of the day, and the day, in most of our lives, is already too much. The dark has become a small luxury, and a thing we almost never enjoy.

The night sky is the test of whether the dark is still doing its work. If you can see the Milky Way, faintly, from your back garden, the dark is doing its work. If you can see only a handful of the brighter stars, the lights are winning. We are not, in this column, going to argue for turning off the lights. We are going to argue for driving, once or twice a year, for forty minutes, to the nearest bit of dark, and standing in it, and looking up. The dark is, in fact, one of the few things that is worth the drive.

![A telescope pointed toward a starry night sky, the kind of small instrument that brings the sky a little closer](https://images.pexels.com/photos/1567069/pexels-photo-1567069.jpeg?auto=compress&cs=tinysrgb&dpr=2&h=650&w=940&w=1800)

## the constellations, and how slowly they change

There is a particular pleasure, when you look up at the sky for more than thirty seconds, in beginning to recognise the constellations. The pleasure is not in any deep astronomical sense. The pleasure is the small, deeply human pleasure of recognising a thing you have not seen in a while. The pleasure is, in some deep way, the same pleasure as recognising a friend in a crowd — the small lift, the small internal nod, the slight feeling of being at home in a place you have not been in a long time.

You do not need to learn the whole sky. You do not need, in any practical sense, to memorise the celestial map, or to be able to point out, with confidence, the difference between Cassiopeia and Cepheus, although the difference between Cassiopeia and Cepheus is worth knowing. You need, in our experience, only two or three anchors — one in the winter sky, one in the summer sky, one that is always there, somewhere above the roofline, no matter what the season. Once you have the anchors, the sky becomes, briefly, a place you know. Once you have the anchors, the sky becomes, in the slow way of all places you know, a place you can return to.

The constellations, also, change slowly. We mean this in two senses. The constellations change, slowly, across the year, in the sense that Orion is a winter constellation, and Cygnus is a summer constellation, and the slow parade of them across the sky is one of the older calendars we have. The constellations also change, slowly, across the centuries, in the sense that the stars themselves are moving, on timescales so long that no human life will see them move by any visible amount. The constellations are, in this sense, the slowest thing in your life. They have been, more or less, the same constellations since the day your grandmother looked up at them, and the day her grandmother looked up at them, and the day her grandmother's grandmother looked up at them. The constellations are, in this sense, the most reliable thing you will ever look at. The constellations are the only subscription in your life that has not, in any visible way, changed since you signed up for it.

## the telescope, and how it is optional

There is, of course, a version of stargazing that involves a telescope. The telescope is a beautiful object. The telescope is, in our experience, the most rewarding piece of equipment a curious adult can own, with the possible exception of a good bread knife. The telescope brings the sky, in a way the naked eye cannot, into focus. The telescope turns the moon, in particular, from a flat disc into a place — a place with mountains, and craters, and shadows, and a horizon you can almost imagine standing on.

We want, however, to argue gently against the idea that the telescope is required. The telescope is, in fact, the second step in the evening, not the first. The first step, and the step that has been doing its work for several thousand years, is the naked eye. The first step is the person, in the dark, looking up, with no equipment, with no app, with no plan. The first step is the part of the evening that has not been improved, in any meaningful way, by the introduction of instruments. The first step is, in fact, slightly diminished by the telescope, in the sense that the telescope gives you a closer view of one thing at the cost of losing the wider view, which is the view we are arguing for here.

The wider view is the view of the sky as a single thing. The wider view is the view that includes, in the same glance, the Milky Way, the seven stars of the Plough, the slow blinking of a satellite, the red eye of a plane, the silver stillness of a moon that has, without your noticing, come up over the roofline. The wider view is the view that makes you feel, briefly, the small, slightly vertiginous thing you are meant to feel when you look up. The wider view is the view that does not need a telescope, and that does not need a guidebook, and that does not need, in fact, anything except the willingness to stand outside, in the dark, for ten minutes, and look up.

The telescope, then, is for later. The telescope is for the night, a few months from now, when you have begun, slowly, to recognise the constellations, and you want, just once, to see, with your own eyes, the rings of Saturn, which is a thing we would not believe, if we had not seen it ourselves, and which we would, very gently, encourage you to see for yourself, at the earliest opportunity. Saturn, through a small telescope, on a clear night, from a back garden, is one of the few experiences that justifies, in our view, the small expense of the telescope.

## the night, as a quiet companion

The night sky is a companion. The night sky is, in fact, one of the older companions we have, and one of the most reliable, and one of the least demanding. The night sky does not require anything of you. The night sky does not require that you understand it, or photograph it, or post about it. The night sky does not require, in fact, that you do anything other than look at it, briefly, on a Tuesday in October, in your socks, in the back garden, before going back inside to do the dishes.

The night sky has, also, the rare quality of being unchanged by being looked at. The mountains, when you visit them, are slightly diminished, in some small way, by the visit. The sky, when you look at it, is exactly as it was before you looked at it, and will be exactly as it was tomorrow night. The sky is the only thing you can look at as often as you like, without it costing anything — not in money, not in carbon, not in any of the small currencies we have been worrying about, lately.

The night sky is, also, a companion in the older sense. The night sky has been, for the entire span of human history, the thing people looked at when they could not sleep. The night sky has been the thing people looked at when they were worried about someone far away. The night sky has been the thing people looked at when they wanted to feel, briefly, that they were small, and that being small was fine. The night sky is the original therapy, and the original therapy has been, for several thousand years, free, and effective, and available without appointment, every clear night, above the roofline.

The walk back inside, after ten minutes in the back garden, is a particular walk. The walk back inside is slower than the walk out. The eyes, having been in the dark, are briefly unable to find the door. The body, having stood outside in the cold, has begun to remember that it was, all along, slightly tired.

You go back inside, and you notice, suddenly, how loud the kitchen is. The fridge is humming. The phone, on the counter, has been accumulating the small urgent notifications of other people's evenings. The kitchen is, suddenly, a lot. The kitchen is, suddenly, the entire modern world, condensed into a small lit room. You stand in the kitchen for a moment, looking at the phone, and you think, briefly, about the sky.

The sky, of course, is still there. The sky is still there, above the roofline, even when you are inside. The sky will be there tonight, and tomorrow night, and the night after that. The sky will be there, in the same way, for the rest of your life, and for the rest of the lives of everyone you love. The sky is the only thing that will not, in any meaningful way, end.

The night sky is the test of whether the dark is still doing its work. If you can see the Milky Way, faintly, from your back garden, the dark is doing its work. If you can see only a handful of the brighter stars, the lights are winning. We are not, in this column, going to argue for turning off the lights. We are going to argue for driving, once or twice a year, for forty minutes, to the nearest bit of dark, and standing in it, and looking up. The dark is, in fact, one of the few things that is worth the drive.

the constellations, and how slowly they change

There is a particular pleasure, when you look up at the sky for more than thirty seconds, in beginning to recognise the constellations. The pleasure is not in any deep astronomical sense. The pleasure is the small, deeply human pleasure of recognising a thing you have not seen in a while. The pleasure is, in some deep way, the same pleasure as recognising a friend in a crowd — the small lift, the small internal nod, the slight feeling of being at home in a place you have not been in a long time.

You do not need to learn the whole sky. You do not need, in any practical sense, to memorise the celestial map, or to be able to point out, with confidence, the difference between Cassiopeia and Cepheus, although the difference between Cassiopeia and Cepheus is worth knowing. You need, in our experience, only two or three anchors — one in the winter sky, one in the summer sky, one that is always there, somewhere above the roofline, no matter what the season. Once you have the anchors, the sky becomes, briefly, a place you know. Once you have the anchors, the sky becomes, in the slow way of all places you know, a place you can return to.

The constellations, also, change slowly. We mean this in two senses. The constellations change, slowly, across the year, in the sense that Orion is a winter constellation, and Cygnus is a summer constellation, and the slow parade of them across the sky is one of the older calendars we have. The constellations also change, slowly, across the centuries, in the sense that the stars themselves are moving, on timescales so long that no human life will see them move by any visible amount. The constellations are, in this sense, the slowest thing in your life. They have been, more or less, the same constellations since the day your grandmother looked up at them, and the day her grandmother looked up at them, and the day her grandmother’s grandmother looked up at them. The constellations are, in this sense, the most reliable thing you will ever look at. The constellations are the only subscription in your life that has not, in any visible way, changed since you signed up for it.

the telescope, and how it is optional

There is, of course, a version of stargazing that involves a telescope. The telescope is a beautiful object. The telescope is, in our experience, the most rewarding piece of equipment a curious adult can own, with the possible exception of a good bread knife. The telescope brings the sky, in a way the naked eye cannot, into focus. The telescope turns the moon, in particular, from a flat disc into a place — a place with mountains, and craters, and shadows, and a horizon you can almost imagine standing on.

We want, however, to argue gently against the idea that the telescope is required. The telescope is, in fact, the second step in the evening, not the first. The first step, and the step that has been doing its work for several thousand years, is the naked eye. The first step is the person, in the dark, looking up, with no equipment, with no app, with no plan. The first step is the part of the evening that has not been improved, in any meaningful way, by the introduction of instruments. The first step is, in fact, slightly diminished by the telescope, in the sense that the telescope gives you a closer view of one thing at the cost of losing the wider view, which is the view we are arguing for here.

The wider view is the view of the sky as a single thing. The wider view is the view that includes, in the same glance, the Milky Way, the seven stars of the Plough, the slow blinking of a satellite, the red eye of a plane, the silver stillness of a moon that has, without your noticing, come up over the roofline. The wider view is the view that makes you feel, briefly, the small, slightly vertiginous thing you are meant to feel when you look up. The wider view is the view that does not need a telescope, and that does not need a guidebook, and that does not need, in fact, anything except the willingness to stand outside, in the dark, for ten minutes, and look up.

The telescope, then, is for later. The telescope is for the night, a few months from now, when you have begun, slowly, to recognise the constellations, and you want, just once, to see, with your own eyes, the rings of Saturn, which is a thing we would not believe, if we had not seen it ourselves, and which we would, very gently, encourage you to see for yourself, at the earliest opportunity. Saturn, through a small telescope, on a clear night, from a back garden, is one of the few experiences that justifies, in our view, the small expense of the telescope.

the night, as a quiet companion

The night sky is a companion. The night sky is, in fact, one of the older companions we have, and one of the most reliable, and one of the least demanding. The night sky does not require anything of you. The night sky does not require that you understand it, or photograph it, or post about it. The night sky does not require, in fact, that you do anything other than look at it, briefly, on a Tuesday in October, in your socks, in the back garden, before going back inside to do the dishes.

The night sky has, also, the rare quality of being unchanged by being looked at. The mountains, when you visit them, are slightly diminished, in some small way, by the visit. The sky, when you look at it, is exactly as it was before you looked at it, and will be exactly as it was tomorrow night. The sky is the only thing you can look at as often as you like, without it costing anything — not in money, not in carbon, not in any of the small currencies we have been worrying about, lately.

The night sky is, also, a companion in the older sense. The night sky has been, for the entire span of human history, the thing people looked at when they could not sleep. The night sky has been the thing people looked at when they were worried about someone far away. The night sky has been the thing people looked at when they wanted to feel, briefly, that they were small, and that being small was fine. The night sky is the original therapy, and the original therapy has been, for several thousand years, free, and effective, and available without appointment, every clear night, above the roofline.

the walk back inside

The walk back inside, after ten minutes in the back garden, is a particular walk. The walk back inside is slower than the walk out. The eyes, having been in the dark, are briefly unable to find the door. The body, having stood outside in the cold, has begun to remember that it was, all along, slightly tired.

You go back inside, and you notice, suddenly, how loud the kitchen is. The fridge is humming. The phone, on the counter, has been accumulating the small urgent notifications of other people’s evenings. The kitchen is, suddenly, a lot. The kitchen is, suddenly, the entire modern world, condensed into a small lit room. You stand in the kitchen for a moment, looking at the phone, and you think, briefly, about the sky.

The sky, of course, is still there. The sky is still there, above the roofline, even when you are inside. The sky will be there tonight, and tomorrow night, and the night after that. The sky will be there, in the same way, for the rest of your life, and for the rest of the lives of everyone you love. The sky is the only thing that will not, in any meaningful way, end.

Step outside tonight. Stand in the dark. Look up. The theater is free. The theater has been running, very patiently, for several billion years. It will run again tomorrow night, provided someone keeps looking up.

Storage, and the Hidden Architecture of a Calm Home
An organized open shelving unit with neatly arranged items
A calm room is not a tidy room — it is a room where every object has a designated seam in the wall, and nothing has to live on the counter.

There is a house I stayed in once, for three weeks one summer, that I have never quite recovered from. It belonged to a friend of a friend, set on a hillside outside a small town, and it had been lived in — patiently, attentively, for nearly thirty years — by a woman who had, over the decades, made peace with every object in it. I noticed this not from the rooms themselves but from the surfaces. There were almost no surfaces. There was no stack of mail on the kitchen counter. There was no pile of shoes by the door. There was no heap of unfolded laundry on the bed. There were, instead, the seams of storage — drawers set into the walls at exactly the height of the objects they were meant to hold, cabinets running deep into the walls in places I would not have thought to put them, a tall cupboard behind a door I had not noticed on the first day, and a low shelf beneath the bench in the hallway that did the work of a coat closet without looking like a coat closet.

I thought about that house for years afterwards. I would come home to my own apartment — my own rooms with their own surfaces, on which my own objects were slowly, inexorably, accumulating — and I would try to remember what, exactly, her house had done that mine did not do. It took me several attempts to articulate it. The difference, I eventually understood, was not that her house was tidier than mine. Tidiness is a temporary achievement, made daily and un-made daily. The difference was that her house had been designed, room by room, over the course of decades, to absorb the objects she owned. My house had been designed to display them. Once I understood this distinction, I could not unsee it.

A calm room is not a tidy room. It is a room where every object has a designated seam in the wall, and nothing has to live on the counter.

![An organized open shelving unit with neatly arranged items](https://images.pexels.com/photos/8580798/pexels-photo-8580798.jpeg?auto=compress&cs=tinysrgb&dpr=2&h=650&w=940&w=1800)

## The Counter Is a Symptom, Not a Surface

We tend to think of the kitchen counter, or the desk, or the console by the door, as a surface — a piece of furniture whose purpose is to hold things. And in a sense it is. But what it is actually doing, in most houses I have visited in the last twenty years, is serving as a confession. The counter is where the objects go that have nowhere else to go. The mail, because there was no shelf narrow enough for it. The keys, because the bowl was on the wrong side of the door. The scissors, because the drawer that used to hold them got re-purposed years ago for takeout menus, and the menus migrated into the junk drawer, and the scissors had to live somewhere, and the counter said yes.

This is not an indictment of the people who live in these houses. Almost every house I know has a counter like this. It is an indictment of the houses themselves, and of the way houses are designed when they are designed at all. Counters are not given enough thought. They are placed by builders in the obvious spots — kitchen, bathroom, hallway — at the standard heights — three feet for the kitchen, two and a half for the hallway — and they are left without any of the surrounding architecture that would have given their objects a home. The house provides a counter. It does not provide, anywhere in the room, a place for the counter's contents.

A calm room, the woman's house taught me, is one in which every object has been asked, at some point in the design of the room: where will you live when you are not in use? The counter is the answer for almost nothing. The counter is the surface for the moment. The drawer is the answer for most things. The drawer is the surface for the rest of the time.

## Why Built-Ins Beat Cabinets

There is an argument to be made for freestanding furniture — the armoire, the sideboard, the tall chest — and it is, on paper, a good argument. These pieces can be moved. They can be inherited. They can follow you from house to house. They can be replaced one at a time, as the room around them evolves. They do not require that the room be reorganized to install them, and they do not require that the room be reorganized again to take them away.

But there is a deeper argument to be made for built-ins, and it is the argument that the woman's house was making. Built-ins are part of the architecture. They are not objects sitting in the room; they are seams in the wall, and the wall has been quietly opened up to receive them. A drawer built into the wall under the stairs sits at exactly the angle of the stairs, and the angle is what makes the drawer possible — the awkward wedge of dead space behind a closed door has become, with the insertion of a shallow drawer, a useful store for shoes, scarves, board games, the things that otherwise would have ended up on the floor of the closet.

This is the heart of what built-ins do. They activate the dead space. Every room has pockets of space that are not reachable from anywhere — the awkward corner behind the door, the strip of wall between the fridge and the end cabinet, the area under the window, the wedge under the stairs. These pockets exist whether or not they are activated. They become part of the room. A built-in is what happens when one of those pockets is recognized as a place something could live.

The house I stayed in that summer had half a dozen of these pockets activated. The drawer under the bench. The shelf behind the door in the kitchen. The shallow cupboard between the fridge and the wall, exactly the depth of a baking sheet. The window seat in the bedroom that lifted up to reveal a cedar chest full of blankets. None of these were large. All of them were specific. Together they subtracted, almost invisibly, the entire problem of the house.

## The Shelf as a Slow Inventory

Once a house has been given enough storage, the question becomes not where things go but what is on the shelves. And this, I think, is the harder question. Storage does not, on its own, declutter a room. It gives clutter a more orderly place to live. The shelves of a room with too much storage still tell the truth about what the room contains, and that truth, if it has not been edited, can be uglier than the truth of the empty counter.

I have come to think of a shelf as a slow inventory. Every item on it is being voted into the room by the person who put it there. The vote is being held every day, in the form of the implicit question: am I still using this? Am I still looking at it? Does it earn the small amount of shelf it occupies? The shelf answers back, with the look of the shelf on a Tuesday afternoon — too low a moment for any pretence — whether the room is proud of the things on it or simply keeping them.

The shelves of the woman's house, like the rest of the room, had been edited slowly, over decades. There were, by my memory, no more than seven objects on any one shelf. Most were the same objects in roughly the same positions that they had occupied three weeks earlier when I arrived. A small ceramic vase from her mother, empty. A wooden bird from a trip to Maine thirty years ago. A photograph in a wooden frame of her husband, who had died in 2009, smiling in a way that meant he was joking with the photographer. The shelves were not curated in any style-conscious sense. They were just the shelves of someone who had kept only what she wanted to keep, and who knew what that was.

This is the part of storage that is about the editing more than the storing. The shelves tell you who you are. They tell you, in time, whether you were serious about the things on them or whether you were merely keeping them out of guilt. A room with excellent storage and poor editing will end up feeling fuller than a room with mediocre storage and good editing. The storage is the easier half of the problem.

## What a Calm House Knows

A calm house knows things. It knows that the books on the bedroom shelf will be read again, and it has made space for them. It knows that the boots by the door will be worn again next week, and it has given them a low shelf instead of letting them queue across the floor. It knows that the luggage will be used three times a year and ignored the rest, and it has put it on the top shelf of a deep closet where it can be reached, but only just. It knows what is coming home from the grocery store, and it has cleared a drawer in the kitchen to receive it before the bags are taken out of the car.

A calm house is not a quiet house. A calm house has the same number of objects in it as any other house. The difference is that the objects have been given places, and the places have been chosen carefully, and the choosing has been done with the understanding that this house is going to be in use for years, and that during those years, every object in it will ask, again and again, whether it still belongs here. The calm house answers those questions patiently. It does not answer them all at once. It just answers them, one at a time, every time an object is returned to its seam in the wall and finds the seam waiting, exactly as it was left.

That, I think, is what the woman's house had, and what mine had been missing. The objects in my own house were all there. They were just not in their seams. They were on the counter, or on the floor, or stacked on the shelf in a way that suggested the shelf had run out of patience. The shelf looked ridiculous for about a week. Then it started to look right. Then I forgot it had ever been otherwise. A year later I had done this in every room of the apartment, one at a time, slowly, until the surfaces had become surfaces again, and the seams had become seams again, and the house had begun, without my noticing, to feel like the house on the hillside.

But it is, in the long run, the architecture that holds everything else up. A home with thoughtful storage can absorb any number of lives. Tailoring, and the Soft Armor of a Well-Fitted Jacket
A tailored blazer hanging on a wooden hanger against a white wall
A jacket that fits at the shoulder is the difference between getting dressed and putting on a posture — a small thing that carries a whole room.

There is a particular feeling, when you put on a jacket that has been fitted to you properly, that no other piece of clothing quite produces. It is not the feeling of being dressed up. It is the feeling of being, in some quiet and almost architectural way, made more usable. The shoulders find their line. The collar settles against the back of the neck. The whole garment does a small, almost invisible thing to your posture — not in a corrective way, not in a disciplinary way, but in the way a well-built room makes the people inside it stand a little more upright without intending to.

This is the strange gift of the tailored jacket. It is a piece of cloth that has been engineered to do something to the person wearing it. And the something it does, when it is fitted correctly, is to give the body a small, soft kind of armor.

Armor is, we think, the right word for it. Not because the jacket is rigid, not because the jacket is severe, not because the jacket is doing anything warlike. But because the jacket has, in its own quiet way, taken on the job of carrying a piece of the weight of being in a room. When you put on a jacket that fits, you are agreeing to let a piece of cloth do part of the work of being seen. You are letting the shoulder speak for you. You are letting the lapel hold the frame of the moment. You are letting the garment take a small share of the responsibility for how the day will go.

And when the jacket fits, you do not notice. You only notice, with relief, that it is doing its job.

![A close-up of a tailored jacket shoulder showing the clean line of the seam and the small ridge of the lapel roll](https://images.pexels.com/photos/31492553/pexels-photo-31492553.jpeg?auto=compress&cs=tinysrgb&dpr=2&h=650&w=940&w=1800)

## The shoulder is the whole sentence

If we had to choose a single measurement on a tailored jacket — a single point on the garment where the entire fit is decided — we would choose the shoulder. Not the chest. Not the waist. Not the sleeve length. The shoulder.

The shoulder is the place where the jacket meets the body. It is the place where the garment ends and the wearer begins. It is the place where the tailor, when cutting the cloth, has decided exactly how the relationship between you and the jacket is going to work. If the shoulder is wrong, the chest will not hang correctly. If the shoulder is right, almost everything else will forgive itself.

A good shoulder does not announce itself. It does not have a sharp seam at the edge of the joint. It does not have a sharp, geometric ridge where the sleeve meets the body. It has, instead, a small, soft transition — the kind of line that you only notice if you are staring at it, and which other people, looking at you across a room, will read as ease. A shoulder like this is the kind of line that says: this person does not need to push against the garment to look like themselves. The garment is pushing back, gently, on their behalf.

A bad shoulder is the opposite. A bad shoulder has a peak at the joint. It has a sharp, slightly geometric edge. It has a small, persistent tension at the seam where the cloth is asking to be somewhere it is not. A bad shoulder is the kind of shoulder you notice in a mirror, in a shop, in the kind of photograph that gets taken at a wedding and never quite recovered. A bad shoulder is the kind of shoulder that makes the wearer, even on a confident day, look slightly unfinished.

This is why, when you are buying a jacket off the rack, the shoulder is the thing to begin with. The shoulder is the thing that cannot be altered. Everything else — the sleeve, the chest, the waist, the length — can be taken in or let out by a competent tailor. The shoulder cannot. The shoulder, on the day you bought the jacket, is the shoulder you are committing to wearing.

## A small history, written in worsted

The tailored jacket, as we know it now, is a relatively recent invention. It is, properly speaking, a piece of clothing that was put together by English country tailors in the middle of the nineteenth century, and then almost immediately transplanted into the wardrobes of cities around the world. Its origins are in riding and in hunting. Its current uses are mostly in meetings.

But what has not changed, in the hundred and seventy-odd years since the jacket became the basic unit of adult dress, is the way it is built. A tailored jacket is still, to this day, built from the inside out. Technology as a Design Object, and the Quiet Joy of a Well-Made Tool on the Desk
A minimalist desk setup with a slim aluminum monitor, a small plant, and natural wood tones
How a generation came to treat its devices like art objects — and what that ambivalent reverence reveals.

Walk into any well-designed apartment of the last decade and you will notice, before the sofa, before the art, a small altar on the desk. A laptop, closed, with its maker's logo catching the light like a tiny chapel window. A phone, face down, in a leather cradle. Perhaps a pair of headphones coiled with the care of a rosary. The objects are not being used at this moment, and yet they are clearly on display. They are not appliances. They are part of the room's vocabulary of taste.

We have, without quite noticing, begun treating our electronics the way earlier generations treated their watches, their pens, their pipes — as small monuments to a kind of life one is trying to live. The mid-century desk of a writer or a designer was a stage set for a certain kind of cultivated selfhood; the same is now true of the writer who keeps only a clear desk, a single lamp, and one beautiful machine at the center of it. The technology has, in a curious reversal, become the still life.

![A close-up of a mechanical keyboard and a ceramic mug on a sunlit windowsill](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1657723212291-aa4c831f9add?crop=entropy&cs=tinysrgb&w=1600&q=80)

## Material Culture in Aluminum

There was a time when a computer was a beige box behind a desk, judged almost entirely by its function, the way a refrigerator is judged. That era, surprisingly recent, is over. The iMac G4, the original MacBook Air, the first Kindle — each of these was a moment when the consumer technology industry discovered that the body of the device could be an argument. The case could be a color. The seam could be a thesis. The weight in the hand could be a verdict on the era that made it.

Design historians call this *material culture*, which is a polite way of saying that objects are never just objects. A room furnished with mid-century modern is making a statement; a room furnished with brass and velvet is making a different one; a room furnished only with a single beautiful screen, a single beautiful lamp, and a single beautiful chair is making a third, and it is this third that has come to feel native to our period. The clean desk, the soft white desk lamp, the discreet speaker — these compose what one might call a monastic aesthetic of technology. It is no accident that so many product photographs now resemble the inside of a chapel.

The reverence is genuine, and not entirely irrational. When the software on these devices changes every week, when the news cycle around them never rests, when the underlying business model of the industry is occasionally something to be uneasy about, the physical object offers a kind of constancy. The aluminum does not pivot. The weight in the hand remains. The hinge still opens with the same soft resistance. In an age of accelerated obsolescence, the design object is one of the last things one can reliably *keep*.

This is, we suspect, why the aesthetics of our devices have moved in the direction they have — toward the matte, the seamless, the nearly seamless, the quietly architectural. The design language of the high-end smartphone, with its rounded corners and its symmetrical cameras and its glass back, is the design language of a small smooth stone. It asks to be held. It declines to advertise its contents. It is, in some hard-to-articulate way, *closed* — a thing with surfaces rather than a thing with features. The user can take a kind of contemplative pleasure in the object precisely because the object refuses, politely, to display its own interiority. It is, like a good poem, an object in which what is hidden is at least as important as what is shown.

## The Quiet Theology of Industrial Design

Look, for a moment, at the design of a high-end pair of headphones, or a flagship camera body, or a brushed-steel desk lamp. There is something almost devotional in the engineering. The tolerances are tighter than they need to be. The surfaces are finished with a care that has nothing to do with function. The packaging itself is designed as if the unboxing were a small liturgy. We are, whether we admit it or not, in the presence of an industrial theology — a faith that good form can dignify the user, that the right object in the right hand can elevate an ordinary afternoon into something composed.

The temptation to overstate this is real, and we should resist it. The aluminum and the glass are, finally, just aluminum and glass. The product photographer has used the same five lighting tricks everyone else has used. The object will, within a year or two, be replaced by another object of approximately the same appearance. The aesthetic religion of the design object is, in the end, a religion of modest miracles: the slightly softer click of the volume button, the slightly more pleasing curve of the lid, the slightly more satisfying weight in the hand. These are real pleasures. They are also small ones. The danger is in confusing the small pleasures with a spiritual practice.

The danger of this reverence is that it can shade into a kind of cosplay. One begins to acquire the objects not for what they do but for what they say about the kind of person who owns them. The taste becomes a costume, and the costume begins to demand upkeep. The desk must be kept clean for the laptop to look right. The cables must be hidden for the lamp to read as art. The room is no longer lived in; it is curated.

There is also, beneath all this, a slightly uncomfortable inheritance. Most of our beautifully designed objects are made, in whole or in part, in places where the workers who made them would not themselves be able to afford to furnish a room with the result. The aluminum is gorgeous; the mine it came from is not. The glass is flawless; the supply chain behind it is something we would rather not sketch on a whiteboard. The aesthetic of the clean desk is, often enough, a triumph of design that quietly brackets the question of who paid for it.

We do not raise this to scold. The contradiction is genuinely structural — it is a feature, not a bug, of a globalized design economy in which the wealthy consume the labor of the less wealthy and the consumption is laundered, in part, through the language of taste. But it is worth holding both things in mind at once. The object on the desk is beautiful. The world that produced the object is not entirely so. The good reader of design, like the good reader of poetry, is the one who can hold the two together without collapsing either into the other.

## What the Object Wants

A good design object, we are told, disappears into the use. This is the old Bauhaus idea — the tool that becomes invisible in the hand. But our technology has a peculiar habit of refusing to disappear. It wants to be looked at, charged, updated, dusted. It wants to be on the desk when guests arrive. It wants its corner of the room. In this sense, our devices are not quite tools and not quite furniture but something in between: objects that participate in our lives as companions do, with their own quiet demands.

This is why, we suspect, the relationship many of us have with our favorite devices has begun to shade, slowly, into something closer to affection. We name them, sometimes — *the old MacBook*, *the work laptop*, *the camera* — in the way one names a small boat or a piano. We feel slightly guilty when we replace them, even when the replacement is materially better. We keep, in a drawer somewhere, the previous generation, the way one keeps old letters. None of this is rational. All of it is, we think, deeply human.

We are, perhaps, in a transitional moment. The next generation of devices — smaller, more ambient, more embroidered into the walls and the wrists and the cars — will not lend themselves to altars in quite the same way. The phone, as a single hand-held object one places on a charging pad at night, may be the high-water mark of technology as a discrete still-life subject. Already, the screens are disappearing into the walls; soon the cameras will be too.

What will remain, we suspect, is not the device but the *impulse* — the human desire to surround oneself with a small number of beautifully made things and to live, however imperfectly, inside the gesture of having chosen them. That impulse is older than any of this technology, and it is one of the better things we do. It is what makes the difference between a room that is merely occupied and a room that is inhabited. And it is, in the end, a thing that no algorithm, however elegant, can do for us.

It has been a picture of what a face could be made to look like if every irregularity were politely erased. The pores have been blurred. The fine lines have been filled. The slight unevenness of tone - which is what skin looks like when it is actually skin - has been smoothed into a kind of luminous porcelain that does not exist outside of a screen. We have become so accustomed to looking at this version of a face that the version we encounter in the mirror, in the morning, in the unforgiving light of our own bathroom, can feel like a failure of maintenance. It is not a failure. It is a face.

There is a quiet shift happening in how we talk about skin. It is not finished. It is not yet universal. But it is real. More and more, the photographs that circulate are photographs of faces that look like faces - with their texture intact, with their pores visible, with the small asymmetries that make a face a face rather than a template. The conversation that is slowly replacing the conversation about perfection is a conversation about texture. About what skin actually looks like. About why this is interesting, and why this is enough.

![A close-up of natural skin in soft window light](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1755540735799-0a0f04cc6894?crop=entropy&cs=tinysrgb&w=1800&q=82)

## What a pore is

Let us begin with the pore, since the pore has been at the center of the beauty conversation for too long. A pore is not a flaw. A pore is the visible opening of a hair follicle, and we have roughly five million of them on the face, give or take. They are not, in any meaningful sense, optional. They are how the skin breathes. They are how the skin releases the small amount of sebum it needs to keep itself supple. They are part of the architecture.

What changes over time is not that we suddenly develop pores, but that they become, with age and with sun damage and with the slow loss of the collagen that once held them tightly closed, more visible. The pore does not grow. The skin around the pore loses some of its tautness, and the pore, which was always there, simply becomes easier to see. This is a normal part of having skin for a long time. It is also, we are now beginning to understand, not something that needs to be concealed.

There has been a multi-billion-dollar industry built around the goal of making pores less visible. Primers blur them. Toners claim to shrink them. Treatments promise to refine them. None of them, in any honest clinical sense, makes the pore go away - because the pore cannot go away. What they do, sometimes, is make the surrounding skin slightly more hydrated, which makes the pore slightly less conspicuous. This is fine. There is nothing wrong with this. But the framing - that the pore is a problem to be solved - is the framing that is starting to shift.

## The geography of a real face

If you look closely at any face that has not been filtered - including, ideally, your own - you will notice that the skin is not one thing. It is a landscape. There is the smoother skin of the cheekbone. There is the slightly oilier T-zone, the forehead and the nose and the chin. There is the thinner, more transparent skin under the eyes, where the capillaries are close enough to the surface that the faintest bruise shows. There are the small brown macules that appear, for many of us, in our thirties and forties, and that are not freckles and not blemishes and not, in any medical sense, problems. There is the faint unevenness of tone across the lower cheek, where the skin has been touched, over the years, by every expression we have made.

None of this is damage. Most of it is not aging, in the catastrophic sense the word has come to carry. It is texture. It is the actual record of having had a face in the world for the number of years we have had one. To pretend otherwise - to insist, as the beauty industry has insisted for decades, that the appropriate response to a real face is to render it invisible - is to commit a particular kind of violence against the body.

This is not to say that there is no place for skincare. There is. The skin is an organ, and like every organ, it benefits from being treated with attention. SPF matters, as does a sensible relationship with the sun. Hydration matters, as does a reasonable amount of sleep. What is changing is the goal. The goal is no longer to make the skin look like nothing. The goal is to make the skin look like itself.

## The influence of the filtered face

It is worth pausing on the filter, because no one fully understood, when the technology arrived, what it would do to the collective idea of beauty. The face filter was a piece of code, originally meant as a playful augmentation of the selfie. Within a few years, it had quietly recalibrated what millions of people thought a face should look like. The "no filter" selfie, paradoxically, became the bold statement. The not-moderated face, in a feed full of smoothed ones, became the provocation.

We are still in the early stages of reckoning with this. There is research, now, suggesting that heavy use of face-altering filters is associated with a measurable shift in how satisfied people are with their own faces - a kind of mirror effect in which the filtered image, having been seen so often, becomes the image against which the unfiltered face is judged. The face in the mirror cannot, by definition, look like the face on the screen. The face in the mirror is not, in fact, failing. The screen is the place where the failure has been engineered.

What we are seeing, in the slow turn of the conversation, is the beginning of an opposite move. Real faces are being shown again, on magazine covers, on runways, on the feeds of the most influential figures in beauty. The pores are visible. The lines are visible. The asymmetry is visible. The faces look like skin, and we are slowly remembering what skin actually looks like.

## What texture does, photographically

There is also a craft truth about texture, and it has to do with why the pictures of real faces are, when we look at them carefully, more compelling than the pictures of filtered ones. A face that has been smoothed is a face that has lost most of what photographs are good at capturing. Photographs, even digital photographs, are best at conveying small variations in light and surface. They reward detail. They reward the faint shadow at the corner of the eye. They reward the slight unevenness of a real cheekbone. A filtered face is a face that has had most of what is photographable taken out of it. We are left with the broad shapes, and we wonder why the picture feels flat.

A face with texture is a face that has something to say to the camera. The light behaves differently on different parts of it. The eye moves. The viewer stays. This is one of the reasons the great portraits of the twentieth century, which were almost entirely unfiltered, still hold us. The texture is what makes the face a face rather than a diagram.

This is not an argument against makeup, or against lighting, or against any of the small adjustments we make when we want to be photographed at our best. It is an argument for the recognition that the adjustments are adjustments - and that the thing being adjusted is more interesting than the adjustment.

## Living in our own faces

The deepest shift, perhaps, is the one that has to happen in the bathroom mirror. The screen filter taught us, for a generation, that the appropriate response to our own face was to find fault. The looking we learned was not the looking we wanted. It was the looking of someone trying to identify what was wrong.

The looking we are learning, slowly, is different. It is the looking of someone trying to notice what is there. The faint line at the corner of the eye, which was there even when we were twenty-two and only became visible later, is not a sign of damage. It is a sign of having made the expressions. The slight unevenness of the cheek is not a flaw. It is the face we have, in a real light, on a real day. The pores are not a problem to be solved. They are the architecture of a skin that is, in its essential design, working as intended.

This shift does not require abandoning skincare. It does not require buying anything, or throwing anything out. It requires only that we look at the faces we have, in the mirrors we have, with the slightly more patient eyes of someone who has finally stopped asking them to be other than they are. The face in the mirror is, in fact, the face. We should try, after some years of asking it to be something else, to find it interesting on its own terms.

There is a version of beauty, in other words, that does not require the face to disappear. It requires the face to be there, with its texture intact, in all the light we can stand. This is the version we are slowly remembering how to want.

The Tote Bag, and the Carryall That Replaced a Closet
A worn leather tote bag sitting on a wooden chair
A good tote is half a handbag and half a confession — everything you might need today, carried in the softest leather you can find.

There is a tote bag on the chair by the door. It has been on the chair by the door, in roughly the same position, for long enough that the chair has begun to remember it. The leather, which started life a pale, almost foal-like tan, has gone the color of strong tea. The handles have darkened where the hand has lived. There is a small ink stain on the inside, near the seam, from a pen that leaked one Tuesday and was never quite cleaned. And the bag itself, even empty, has taken on the slightly slumped, slightly weighted posture of a thing that is rarely completely empty, and is rarely completely full, and is rarely asked to be either.

This is the strange and rather wonderful thing about a really good tote. It is, in the most literal sense, a piece of architecture for carrying things. But it is also, in a less literal sense, a small piece of autobiography. The tote bag is the piece of your wardrobe that contains, at any given hour, the working evidence of how you actually live. There is the notebook, slightly bent from being carried too long. There is the small tin of something that you keep meaning to throw out. There is the pair of sunglasses you lost three months ago and which reappeared, last week, at the very bottom. There is the receipt from the lunch you had on Tuesday and which, for reasons you cannot quite explain, you have not thrown away. There is the book you have been meaning to finish, the pen you have been meaning to replace, the charger that works with exactly one device and which is, for this reason, indispensable.

The tote is the place where all of those things go. The tote is the place where the day, in its small and rather ordinary way, has been agreeing to live.

![A close-up of a softly worn leather tote with a notebook and small objects peeking out from its open top, on a wooden floor in afternoon light](https://images.pexels.com/photos/6787035/pexels-photo-6787035.jpeg?auto=compress&cs=tinysrgb&dpr=2&h=650&w=940&w=1800)

## The bag that was not a handbag

It is worth pausing for a moment to notice that the tote bag, in the modern sense, was not always a thing that women carried. The tote began, as best anyone can tell, as a piece of equipment — an open-topped bag made of heavy canvas, sometimes leather, designed for carrying things that a smaller bag could not. The ice went to market in a tote. The library books came home in a tote. The groceries, before the era of the small cart and the large car, were carried up the front walk in a tote.

The tote was, in other words, a piece of utility. It was not, in any sense, a piece of fashion. And this is, we think, the secret of why the tote still works in a way that the more elegant handbag sometimes does not. The tote did not begin as an object of desire. It began as an object of use. And this means that when you pick one up, even today, you are picking up a bag that is not asking to be admired. The tote is a bag that has agreed to be helpful.

This is also why the tote has, in the last ten or fifteen years, returned so thoroughly to the center of the modern wardrobe. There was a long stretch, in the nineties and the two-thousands, when the small, very structured, very expensive handbag was the dominant object of the working wardrobe. These bags had a job to do, and the job was to be beautiful. They were beautiful, mostly. They were also almost impossible to carry a paperback in.

The tote has come back, we think, because we have stopped, at last, pretending that we live the kind of life that fits into a small bag. We have stoppers, we have snacks, we have chargers, we have small children. We have weather. We have books we are reading and books we are saving to read. We have, in short, things. And the tote, more than almost any other bag, has agreed to hold them.

## What the day looks like, packed in cloth

There is an Italian expression, non so dove, which roughly translates as I don't know where, and which is what the Italian person says when they have forgotten where they put something. The Italian tote bag, when made honestly, is the cure for non so dove. The Italian tote knows where things go. The Italian tote has, in its soft architecture, places for each of the things you are likely to need in a day. There is the long inner pocket for the laptop. There is the smaller outer pocket for the phone. There is the place for the keys, the place for the wallet, the place for the thing you keep meaning to mail. The tote, when it is well-designed, has a small geography. The tote, when it is yours, has a small geography you already know.

This is the second secret of the tote. The first is that it is, by history, a bag of use. The second is that the bag of use, over time, becomes a kind of organized drawer. The tote develops, in the way that every well-loved container develops, a particular order. Not the order of somebody else's design. The order of yours. The order, in fact, that has been slowly negotiated between you and your days, over the last three years, every time you have reached into the bag for something and found it.

This is also why changing a tote, after a few years of loyalty to the old one, is such a strange and slightly melancholy undertaking. You are not just changing a bag. You are changing the geography where you keep the small, working evidence of how you live. The new tote will, in time, develop its own geography. But for a few weeks, you will be reaching into the wrong pockets. You will be looking, by reflex, for the pen on the left side, and finding it on the right. The transition, like the transition between one apartment and another, is a small grief.

It is worth saying that this grief is also, eventually, a kind of pleasure. The tote, like any good piece of architecture, will adapt to its occupant. The new tote will, within a season, have become the old tote. The new tote will have its own ink stain, its own telling place. The relationship will rebuild itself. But the rebuilding, like all rebuildings, takes a moment.

## The leather is the long conversation

If we had to choose a single material from which a tote should be made, we would choose leather. Not because canvas does not work. Canvas, in fact, works very well. But because leather, in the way that almost no other material does, agrees to age with you.

A canvas tote is, by its nature, a kind of seasonal bag. It is the bag you take to the market in June. It is the bag you put in the corner of the closet when the weather turns. It does not have a long biography. It does not develop a patina. It does not become more interesting the longer you carry it. The canvas tote is, in this sense, a young bag. It is the bag you keep for a year or two before passing on.

A leather tote is the opposite. A leather tote, if you have chosen it with any care at all, will be the bag you are still carrying in a decade. It will go dark at the handles. It will soften at the corners. It will pick up a small mark on the front, from the day you put it down too hard on the bench at the cafe, and it will keep that mark forever. The leather will, slowly, agree to take the shape of your shoulder. The leather will, in the end, become something you cannot quite imagine replacing.

This is the long conversation that leather has with the person carrying it. The conversation is slow. The conversation is sometimes a little costly. The conversation will, however, outlast any number of trend bags.

### the small things to look for

If you are buying a leather tote this season — and we will say only that, in our experience, most people who have not already bought one are, at some point, going to — there are a few small things worth attending to.

Look, first, at the handle attachment. The handles should be sewn into the bag, not riveted. A riveted handle is a handle that is, statistically, more likely to come loose in the third year. A sewn handle is a handle that has been attached the way a tailor would attach it, and which will, with reasonable care, be the handle that is still there in the tenth year.

Look, second, at the lining. The lining, ideally, should be a piece of cloth, not a piece of plastic. A cotton lining will, over time, settle into the bag in a way that a synthetic one will not. A cotton lining will let you find things by feel. A cotton lining will, after a season, have taken on the particular smell of whatever you keep in the bag — which is, in our view, a feature and not a bug.

Look, third, at the strap. The strap, on a tote that you intend to carry for any length of time, should be wide enough to sit on a shoulder without cutting. It should be soft enough at the edges to fold slightly. It should not, by any means, be the kind of strap that leaves a small red mark on a bare shoulder at the end of an hour. A bag that is comfortable to carry is a bag you will, in fact, carry. A bag that is uncomfortable to carry is a bag that ends up on the chair by the door.

## A confession, in soft leather

The tote bag, in the end, is a confession. It is the piece of your wardrobe that admits, more honestly than anything else, to the kind of life you actually live. A small, elegant handbag is the kind of bag that says you live the kind of life where you leave the house with nothing but a credit card and a phone. A tote is the kind of bag that says you live the kind of life where you leave the house prepared.

This is, when you stop to think about it, the more interesting confession. The tote is, in a small way, an argument against the modern fantasy of minimalism. The tote is, in fact, the bag that has been allowed to be maximal. The tote is allowed to be a little heavy. The tote is allowed to slump on one side because there is a thermos in it. The tote is allowed to have a small stain, a small ink mark, a small corner of notebook peeking out.

The tote is the bag of the person who has, somewhere along the way, stopped trying to be a curated object. It is the bag of the person who has agreed, quietly and without announcement, to be a real one. And this is, we think, why we keep coming back to the tote year after year, and why we find that the tote, even when we have bought another bag, is the one we still reach for.

It is the bag that knows what we need before we do. It is the bag that has, in some quiet way, made room for the day. And it is the bag, when we get home at night and put it back on the chair by the door, that sits there waiting, patiently, for the next morning, when we will reach for it again, and it will be exactly where we left it. It will be the same bag it was the day we bought it. And it will also, by then, be a slightly different bag. The leather will have softened another fraction. The handles will have darkened another fraction. The pocket will hold, in a slightly different position, the small working evidence of how the day has been.

This is the long conversation of the tote. This is what it knows. And this is why, of all the bags in the closet, the tote is the one we would have the most trouble doing without.

You are changing the geography where you keep the small, working evidence of how you live. The new tote will, in time, develop its own geography. But for a few weeks, you will be reaching into the wrong pockets. You will be looking, by reflex, for the pen on the left side, and finding it on the right. The transition, like the transition between one apartment and another, is a small grief.

It is worth saying that this grief is also, eventually, a kind of pleasure. The tote, like any good piece of architecture, will adapt to its occupant. The new tote will, within a season, have become the old tote. The new tote will have its own ink stain, its own telling place. The relationship will rebuild itself. But the rebuilding, like all rebuildings, takes a moment.

The leather is the long conversation

If we had to choose a single material from which a tote should be made, we would choose leather. Not because canvas does not work. Canvas, in fact, works very well. But because leather, in the way that almost no other material does, agrees to age with you.

A canvas tote is, by its nature, a kind of seasonal bag. It is the bag you take to the market in June. It is the bag you put in the corner of the closet when the weather turns. It does not have a long biography. It does not develop a patina. It does not become more interesting the longer you carry it. The canvas tote is, in this sense, a young bag. It is the bag you keep for a year or two before passing on.

A leather tote is the opposite. A leather tote, if you have chosen it with any care at all, will be the bag you are still carrying in a decade. It will go dark at the handles. It will soften at the corners. It will pick up a small mark on the front, from the day you put it down too hard on the bench at the cafe, and it will keep that mark forever. The leather will, slowly, agree to take the shape of your shoulder. The leather will, in the end, become something you cannot quite imagine replacing.

This is the long conversation that leather has with the person carrying it. The conversation is slow. The conversation is sometimes a little costly. The conversation will, however, outlast any number of trend bags.

the small things to look for

If you are buying a leather tote this season — and we will say only that, in our experience, most people who have not already bought one are, at some point, going to — there are a few small things worth attending to.

Look, first, at the handle attachment. The handles should be sewn into the bag, not riveted. A riveted handle is a handle that is, statistically, more likely to come loose in the third year. A sewn handle is a handle that has been attached the way a tailor would attach it, and which will, with reasonable care, be the handle that is still there in the tenth year.

Look, second, at the lining. The lining, ideally, should be a piece of cloth, not a piece of plastic. A cotton lining will, over time, settle into the bag in a way that a synthetic one will not. A cotton lining will let you find things by feel. A cotton lining will, after a season, have taken on the particular smell of whatever you keep in the bag — which is, in our view, a feature and not a bug.

Look, third, at the strap. The strap, on a tote that you intend to carry for any length of time, should be wide enough to sit on a shoulder without cutting. It should be soft enough at the edges to fold slightly. It should not, by any means, be the kind of strap that leaves a small red mark on a bare shoulder at the end of an hour. A bag that is comfortable to carry is a bag you will, in fact, carry. A bag that is uncomfortable to carry is a bag that ends up on the chair by the door.

A confession, in soft leather

The tote bag, in the end, is a confession. It is the piece of your wardrobe that admits, more honestly than anything else, to the kind of life you actually live. A small, elegant handbag is the kind of bag that says you live the kind of life where you leave the house with nothing but a credit card and a phone. A tote is the kind of bag that says you live the kind of life where you leave the house prepared.

This is, when you stop to think about it, the more interesting confession. The tote is, in a small way, an argument against the modern fantasy of minimalism. The tote is, in fact, the bag that has been allowed to be maximal. The tote is allowed to be a little heavy. The tote is allowed to slump on one side because there is a thermos in it. The tote is allowed to have a small stain, a small ink mark, a small corner of notebook peeking out.

The tote is the bag of the person who has, somewhere along the way, stopped trying to be a curated object. It is the bag of the person who has agreed, quietly and without announcement, to be a real one. And this is, we think, why we keep coming back to the tote year after year, and why we find that the tote, even when we have bought another bag, is the one we still reach for.

It is the bag that knows what we need before we do. It is the bag that has, in some quiet way, made room for the day. And it is the bag, when we get home at night and put it back on the chair by the door, that sits there waiting, patiently, for the next morning, when we will reach for it again, and it will be exactly where we left it. It will be the same bag it was the day we bought it. And it will also, by then, be a slightly different bag. The leather will have softened another fraction. The handles will have darkened another fraction. The pocket will hold, in a slightly different position, the small working evidence of how the day has been.

This is the long conversation of the tote. This is what it knows. And this is why, of all the bags in the closet, the tote is the one we would have the most trouble doing without.
