Walking as a Modern Practice, and the Slow Return of Going Nowhere in Particular
A solitary figure walking down a misty morning street, soft golden light
Walking is the only practice left that asks nothing of us but our presence.

There is a particular hour in the morning — not yet eight, the sun still low and a little cautious — when the city has a thin, translucent quality, like a page that has not yet been written on. The shopkeepers are lifting their shutters, the dog walkers have already finished their rounds, and a few of us slip along the sidewalk at the pace the body has always wanted to move. We are not exercising. We are not optimising. We are walking.

This is an old activity. Humans have done it for something like six million years, and we have done it well enough to colonise every continent on earth by foot. The first poems were probably composed while walking, the first myths were probably invented while walking, and most of what we call thinking is in fact the residue of a body in motion. Yet somewhere in the last fifty years, walking became something we had to justify. We began to wear the right shoes for it. We began to count the steps. We began to call it cardio.

![Walking alone down a quiet tree-lined street at first light](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1541659403003-a58d37b4c697?crop=entropy&cs=tinysrgb&w=1600&q=80)

## The Pace That Thinks

A walking pace is a strange thing. It is the only speed at which the world refuses to be abstracted. In a car, the city is a sequence of green lights and brake lights; on a bicycle, it is a problem of right-of-way; on a train, it is a moving painting. But at walking pace, the city is intimate. You notice the iron grillwork above the bakery door. You notice the way a woman carries a paper bag of croissants like she is holding something tender. You notice, suddenly, that the pharmacy has painted its shutters a colour you have liked, for years, without ever naming.

This is not nostalgia, although it sometimes feels close. It is a particular mode of attention that the body gives you when it is not being asked to do anything else. Philosophers from Thoreau to Rousseau to Agnes Varda have written about it. Rebecca Solnit made it the subject of an entire book. But the practice does not really require their permission. You can simply step out of your door tomorrow morning, leave the phone in your pocket, and walk for forty minutes in any direction. Something will happen in your head. It almost always does.

The contemporary mind is built around interruption. We have trained ourselves to be available at any moment, to fragment attention across dozens of small tasks, to believe that efficiency is a moral virtue. Walking is the opposite of this. Walking cannot be efficiently done. It takes what it takes. The slower you go, the more you see. The more you see, the slower you want to go. There is a kind of soft negotiation with the world happening all the time, and we have almost entirely forgotten that it is available to us for free.

## The Body as a Returning Thing

When we walk, the body does something it has stopped doing in the rest of our lives: it becomes the source of perception rather than its container. We usually treat the body as the vehicle that carries the head around. The head is doing the work; the body is just along for the ride. Walking reverses this. Suddenly the head has to follow the legs. The legs have to find the curb, the puddle, the loose paving stone. The lungs have to do their patient bellows work. The skin registers the weather.

There is a humbling that happens in this. The body, which we have been ignoring for hours or days, begins to reassert itself in the most gentle way. The ache in the calf that you had not noticed. The particular way the right hip tightens after a night of bad sleep. The hunger, real hunger, that arrives around minute twenty. These are not warnings. They are the body reminding you that it is here, that it has been here all along, that it has feelings and opinions and rhythms which your opinions about it had temporarily obscured.

I think this is one of the great secret gifts of walking. It returns us to ourselves in the only way that still works: by making us inhabit the body instead of thinking about it. We don't have to do anything with this knowledge. We don't have to journal about it, or post about it, or measure it. We just have to keep walking, and let the body be the body, and let the mind follow where the feet go.

## A Practice Without Metrics

The reason I want to call walking a practice, rather than a workout, is because practices don't have endpoints. A practice is something you return to. It is something that changes you slowly, without announcement, like the way a path is gradually worn into a lawn. You don't finish a practice. You simply do it again tomorrow, and again the day after, and one day you realise you are a person who walks. That is the entire transformation.

The wellness industry has spent the last decade trying to make walking into something measurable. There are watches for it. There are apps for it. There are competitions among friends, step goals, streaks, badges. None of this is harmful, exactly. But none of it is what walking actually is. Walking is the activity you do when you have stopped trying to turn yourself into a project. Walking is what is left when you have given up, briefly, on self-improvement.

This is why I find it strange that we have so few occasions to walk without purpose. We walk to get somewhere, or we walk to log a number, or we walk because the dog needs to walk. But the practice — the real practice — is the walk without an argument. You step out at a particular time, you go in a particular direction, you come back when you come back. No one is waiting for you at the end of it. You are not delivering yourself anywhere. You are simply letting the hours pass through you, and the streets pass through you, and the seasons pass through you, one footfall at a time.

I have come to think of this as a kind of slow citizenship. The walker knows the city in a way the driver never can, and the cyclist only halfway. The walker knows which streets smell like bread in the morning, and which blocks hold their warmth a little longer after sundown. The walker has favourite cracks in the pavement, favourite cats, favourite trees that have grown taller since last spring. None of this is on the map. None of it can be monetised. But it is the texture of a life, and it is what we lose when we stop walking.

There is, too, a small political dimension to this. The walker is the citizen the city is built for. Every curb cut, every traffic-calmed intersection, every shady street tree, every plaza with a bench that actually faces something worth looking at — these are the result of decades of slow, unglamorous work by people who believed that cities should be walkable. The walker, by walking, ratifies that work. Every step is a quiet vote for the kind of city in which walking is possible, and against the kind of city in which it has become an afterthought. This is not activism. It is something gentler than activism, and more durable. It is the daily practice of being the kind of person for whom the city was designed, and by being that person, reminding the city what it was supposed to be.

You will simply walk, and notice, and think, and arrive back at your door forty minutes later feeling like you have slept an extra hour. That feeling is the practice. It is not dramatic. It is not shareable. It is the oldest gift the body has ever offered the mind, and it is still available, this morning, on every block in every city in the world, to anyone who is willing to go a little slower than the world is asking them to.

It does not keep a streak. The only thing it asks is that we return to it, eventually, with the same modest willingness we brought to it the first time. The morning is always there. The streets are always there. The feet, with a little luck, are always there.

The Wardrobe as an Archive, and the Quiet Art of Keeping What You Have Already Lived In
A row of vintage coats hanging in a sunlit closet
The pieces we keep across decades — the coat from the first job, the bag from the trip — are how we carry our history.

There is a coat at the back of our closet that our mother wore to her first job, in the late 1980s. It is a long, dark wool coat with a single-breasted cut and buttons that were, originally, very dark brown. The buttons are now slightly lighter than the cloth, because the cloth has darkened a little with age and the buttons have not. The shoulders fit no one in the family. The sleeves are an inch too long for everyone. But it has hung in this closet for thirty years, and we cannot quite bring ourselves to send it anywhere else.

It is not a particularly beautiful coat. It was not expensive when it was bought. It does not flatter anyone in the way fashion magazines mean the word *flatter*. But it is the coat that was worn to interviews. It is the coat that was worn home from the hospital when our brother was born. It is the coat that was worn, one evening in November, on the way to a dinner where a thing happened that changed the entire course of the family.

The coat is an archive. The coat remembers what we have, mostly, forgotten.

We would argue that this is true of most wardrobes, if we let them be. Most wardrobes, if we stop to think about it, are not really collections of clothes. They are collections of *moments*. They are the small portable archives of who we have been and where we have been and what we have decided mattered. A wardrobe, properly cared for, is a kind of second memory — one that runs alongside the memory in our head, and that often knows things the memory in our head has decided to let go.

![A vintage leather bag resting on a sun-warmed wooden floor beside a folded silk scarf](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1643168661851-199cf2bba5c0?crop=entropy&cs=tinysrgb&w=1600&q=80)

## The coat you still have

It is a peculiar and rather lovely thing, the way a wardrobe can outlive the person who began it. Our grandmother's wardrobe is in this house, somewhere, even though she has been gone for fifteen years. There are the housecoats she wore in the kitchen in the late afternoon. There are the three pairs of wool trousers she wore to bridge club every Thursday for forty years. There are the scarves. We could not, at this point, count the scarves. They are in a small wooden box in the linen closet, each one folded into a perfect square, each one with a faint smell of her perfume that has not, in any honest sense, faded.

We keep these things. We are not quite sure why. They are not, in any functional sense, useful to us. They do not fit our lives. The housecoats would be too short for us by now, and the wool trousers are a style we have never quite learned to wear. The scarves are silk, and they are lovely, but we have our own scarves, and we have not yet reached the point of wearing hers.

But we keep them. Because they are, we have come to understand, a record. They are the small physical proof that a woman existed. That she had taste. That she had a routine. That she wore scarves at the bridge table. That she had opinions about wool. That she answered the door in her housecoat at four in the afternoon, when the light was the kind of light that asked to be let in.

The coat at the back of our closet is the same kind of object. It is small evidence. It is the closet's way of holding on to a woman who is no longer here to be held.

This is what we mean by the archive. Not the museum, and not the heirloom exactly. But the small, ordinary, slightly inconvenient thing that you keep because keeping it is, in some quiet way, a kind of loyalty.

## Objects that outlive the moment

Every piece of clothing that has survived a long time in your wardrobe has, almost by definition, outlived the moment it was made for. The shirt you wore to your graduation. The dress you wore on the holiday where you met the person you eventually married. The shoes you wore to the wedding of a friend who has since stopped being a friend, and which you wore anyway, because they were the right shoes that day and you would rather keep the shoes than lose the day.

These objects have all outlived their usefulness in the narrow sense. They do not, in any literal way, do anything for you now. They are too small, or too dated, or too loaded. You could not, in good conscience, wear the graduation shirt to a meeting. You could not wear the holiday dress to a parent-teacher evening. They belong to a version of you that no longer quite exists in the world.

But they belong to *you*. They are the small physical remainder of those versions. And the day will come, perhaps once every five years, when you open the closet and find the shirt, and you put it on for an evening at home, and for the length of one quiet hour you are again the person who wore it on the day the world changed.

This is the gift of the archive. The archive gives you back the days you thought you had lost. It does so quietly, and only when you ask, and it never quite charges for the service.

We have a friend who keeps a single shoe — just one, from a pair — in the back of her closet. The matching shoe was lost on a beach in Greece in 1996. She has kept the surviving shoe for twenty-eight years. She does not know why. It is not a useful shoe. It is not a beautiful shoe. But it is the small physical remainder of a long-ago August, and she cannot quite bear to put it in the bin.

We would not, in any serious way, call this sentimentality. Sentimentality is when you pretend a thing matters more than it does. This is the opposite. This is admitting, openly, that a single shoe from 1996 matters in a way that goes beyond what a single shoe ought to matter. It is the wardrobe admitting that it has a memory.

## Letting the archive speak

The wardrobe, if you let it, will tell you a great deal about who you have been. We have looked, on quiet afternoons, at the clothes we have kept for twenty years, and we have been slightly surprised by the woman they describe. She is, in some ways, a stranger. She wore colors we would not, today, choose to wear. She wore shapes that look, from this distance, slightly uncertain. She had a taste for beads, and for small floral prints, and for shoes that came to a slightly pointed toe in a way that no longer seems quite right.

But she is also clearly *us*. She is the person who went to certain schools and certain jobs and certain dinner parties. She is the person who lived in certain apartments and read certain books and had certain friends, and who was, in her way, beginning to become the person who would eventually become us. The wardrobe remembers her, even when we do not.

This is what we are asking the wardrobe to do, when we keep things. We are asking it to remember. We are asking it to hold onto the small, ordinary, slightly awkward evidence of who we were, so that we do not have to do all the remembering ourselves. We are asking it to be, in some very practical sense, the second half of the memory.

There is also, we think, a small discipline in this. It is the discipline of not throwing things away simply because they no longer suit the current version of the wardrobe. The white shirt from the first job has earned its place in the drawer. The leather bag from the trip has earned its place on the high shelf. The coat from someone who is no longer here has earned its place at the back of the closet, even if no one will ever quite wear it again.

These objects are not, strictly speaking, part of the wardrobe anymore. They are part of the wardrobe's memory. And they should be allowed to keep their place.

## What the archive asks of us

If the wardrobe is an archive, then it asks a small set of things of us. It asks to be allowed to keep things. It asks to be allowed to remember things. It asks not to be purged, every spring, of every object that has not been worn in a year. It asks to be treated as the small, slow, slightly imperfect record of a life that has been lived.

It also asks, gently, that we stop apologizing for keeping things. There is a particular kind of modern guilt, in our experience, about holding onto clothes we no longer wear. The voice that says *you should not keep things you do not use* is a voice worth listening to, but it is not the only voice. There is another voice, quieter, that says *some things are kept not because they are useful but because they remember*. We would argue that the second voice is the older voice, and that the wardrobe, like the rest of us, is better off when we listen to it.

They are the small, washed, sun-faded, slightly mended proof that we were here, and that we dressed ourselves, and that we walked out into the day, and that we came home again.

When we open the closet on a quiet morning, we are not just choosing an outfit. We are consulting the archive. We are asking it what kind of day we might be willing to have, and what kind of person we might be willing to remember being.

A wardrobe, properly cared for, is a kind of second memory — one that runs alongside the memory in our head, and that often knows things the memory in our head has decided to let go.

The coat you still have

It is a peculiar and rather lovely thing, the way a wardrobe can outlive the person who began it. Our grandmother’s wardrobe is in this house, somewhere, even though she has been gone for fifteen years. There are the housecoats she wore in the kitchen in the late afternoon. There are the three pairs of wool trousers she wore to bridge club every Thursday for forty years. There are the scarves. We could not, at this point, count the scarves. They are in a small wooden box in the linen closet, each one folded into a perfect square, each one with a faint smell of her perfume that has not, in any honest sense, faded.

We keep these things. We are not quite sure why. They are not, in any functional sense, useful to us. They do not fit our lives. The housecoats would be too short for us by now, and the wool trousers are a style we have never quite learned to wear. The scarves are silk, and they are lovely, but we have our own scarves, and we have not yet reached the point of wearing hers.

But we keep them. Because they are, we have come to understand, a record. They are the small physical proof that a woman existed. That she had taste. That she had a routine. That she wore scarves at the bridge table. That she had opinions about wool. That she answered the door in her housecoat at four in the afternoon, when the light was the kind of light that asked to be let in.

The coat at the back of our closet is the same kind of object. It is small evidence. It is the closet’s way of holding on to a woman who is no longer here to be held.

This is what we mean by the archive. Not the museum, and not the heirloom exactly. But the small, ordinary, slightly inconvenient thing that you keep because keeping it is, in some quiet way, a kind of loyalty.

Objects that outlive the moment

Every piece of clothing that has survived a long time in your wardrobe has, almost by definition, outlived the moment it was made for. The shirt you wore to your graduation. The dress you wore on the holiday where you met the person you eventually married. The shoes you wore to the wedding of a friend who has since stopped being a friend, and which you wore anyway, because they were the right shoes that day and you would rather keep the shoes than lose the day.

These objects have all outlived their usefulness in the narrow sense. They do not, in any literal way, do anything for you now. They are too small, or too dated, or too loaded. You could not, in good conscience, wear the graduation shirt to a meeting. You could not wear the holiday dress to a parent-teacher evening. They belong to a version of you that no longer quite exists in the world.

But they belong to you. They are the small physical remainder of those versions. And the day will come, perhaps once every five years, when you open the closet and find the shirt, and you put it on for an evening at home, and for the length of one quiet hour you are again the person who wore it on the day the world changed.

This is the gift of the archive. The archive gives you back the days you thought you had lost. It does so quietly, and only when you ask, and it never quite charges for the service.

We have a friend who keeps a single shoe — just one, from a pair — in the back of her closet. The matching shoe was lost on a beach in Greece in 1996. She has kept the surviving shoe for twenty-eight years. She does not know why. It is not a useful shoe. It is not a beautiful shoe. But it is the small physical remainder of a long-ago August, and she cannot quite bear to put it in the bin.

We would not, in any serious way, call this sentimentality. Sentimentality is when you pretend a thing matters more than it does. This is the opposite. This is admitting, openly, that a single shoe from 1996 matters in a way that goes beyond what a single shoe ought to matter. It is the wardrobe admitting that it has a memory.

Letting the archive speak

The wardrobe, if you let it, will tell you a great deal about who you have been. We have looked, on quiet afternoons, at the clothes we have kept for twenty years, and we have been slightly surprised by the woman they describe. She is, in some ways, a stranger. She wore colors we would not, today, choose to wear. She wore shapes that look, from this distance, slightly uncertain. She had a taste for beads, and for small floral prints, and for shoes that came to a slightly pointed toe in a way that no longer seems quite right.

But she is also clearly us. She is the person who went to certain schools and certain jobs and certain dinner parties. She is the person who lived in certain apartments and read certain books and had certain friends, and who was, in her way, beginning to become the person who would eventually become us. The wardrobe remembers her, even when we do not.

This is what we are asking the wardrobe to do, when we keep things. We are asking it to remember. We are asking it to hold onto the small, ordinary, slightly awkward evidence of who we were, so that we do not have to do all the remembering ourselves. We are asking it to be, in some very practical sense, the second half of the memory.

There is also, we think, a small discipline in this. It is the discipline of not throwing things away simply because they no longer suit the current version of the wardrobe. The white shirt from the first job has earned its place in the drawer. The leather bag from the trip has earned its place on the high shelf. The coat from someone who is no longer here has earned its place at the back of the closet, even if no one will ever quite wear it again.

These objects are not, strictly speaking, part of the wardrobe anymore. They are part of the wardrobe’s memory. And they should be allowed to keep their place.

What the archive asks of us

If the wardrobe is an archive, then it asks a small set of things of us. It asks to be allowed to keep things. It asks to be allowed to remember things. It asks not to be purged, every spring, of every object that has not been worn in a year. It asks to be treated as the small, slow, slightly imperfect record of a life that has been lived.

It also asks, gently, that we stop apologizing for keeping things. There is a particular kind of modern guilt, in our experience, about holding onto clothes we no longer wear. The voice that says you should not keep things you do not use is a voice worth listening to, but it is not the only voice. There is another voice, quieter, that says some things are kept not because they are useful but because they remember. We would argue that the second voice is the older voice, and that the wardrobe, like the rest of us, is better off when we listen to it.

The wardrobe as an archive is a small, modest, slightly inconvenient idea. It is the idea that the things we have worn are not, finally, separate from who we are. They are us, in their way. They are the small, washed, sun-faded, slightly mended proof that we were here, and that we dressed ourselves, and that we walked out into the day, and that we came home again.

When we open the closet on a quiet morning, we are not just choosing an outfit. We are consulting the archive. We are asking it what kind of day we might be willing to have, and what kind of person we might be willing to remember being.

It is, we think, an honor to be consulted this way.

The Weekend Trail, and the Slow Accumulation of Knowing a Single Forest Path
A forest path winding through tall trees in soft morning light
Choosing a single forest path and walking it often — the slow accumulation of knowing a place.

There is a particular trail, not far from my house, that I have walked on a Saturday or a Sunday in most weeks for several years. The trail is six kilometres long, out and back, with a small hill in the middle and a stream at the bottom. The trail is not, in any objective sense, remarkable. It does not appear in any guidebook. It has no view at the top. It is, mostly, just trees, in a row, in a forest, with a path through them.

I have walked this trail in every season. I have walked it in spring, when the trilliums are out and the streams are loud and the forest smells of mud. I have walked it in summer, when the deerflies are out and the leaves are dense and the path is mostly shade. I have walked it in autumn, when the maples turn and the light comes in low and the forest smells, briefly, like a forest in a book. I have walked it in winter, with the snow on the ground and the trees black against the white, and the silence, when the wind drops, is the most complete silence I know.

I mention this trail because I think there is something true about the practice of choosing one trail, and walking it often, that is not true about the practice of walking many trails once. The first kind of walking is what the hiking magazines write about. The second kind is what we actually do, and what, I think, we are secretly trying to do, even when we say we want to do the first kind.

![A forest path under tall trees, soft light filtering through the canopy](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1778837705759-9eb37b05ed6e?crop=entropy&cs=tinysrgb&w=1800&q=82)

## the trail as a place you know

We have, in the modern world, almost lost the idea of a place you know. We have replaced it, instead, with the idea of places you have been. We have been to many places. We have known very few. Knowing a place is different from having been to it. Knowing a place is a long, slow, mostly boring accumulation of small observations, in the same place, over many visits. Knowing a place is what happens when you have walked the same trail enough times that you know, without looking, where the roots are, and where the mud is deepest in spring, and where the squirrels have their dens, and where the light, on a particular morning in early November, comes through the trees at the exact angle that makes the path look like a painting.

This kind of knowing cannot be acquired on a single trip. It cannot be acquired on a single season. It can only be acquired by walking, again and again, in the same place, with the same pair of shoes, and the same small bag, and the same modest attention. It is the kind of knowing that is, I think, what the word practice actually means. Practice is not a single performance. Practice is repetition. Practice is the slow accumulation, over years, of the small observations that become, eventually, a place you know.

There is a particular pleasure in this knowing. The pleasure is hard to describe, because it is not the pleasure of discovery. The pleasure of discovery is what we are usually sold, by travel and by adventure writing. The pleasure of discovery is the pleasure of seeing something new. The pleasure of knowing is the pleasure of seeing something old, in a new way. The pleasure is the pleasure of noticing, on the fifteenth time you have walked past a particular tree, that the tree has grown, slightly, since the last time. The pleasure is the pleasure of noticing that the sapling you pointed out to a friend, three summers ago, is now, in fact, taller than you are. The pleasure is the pleasure of seeing the place change, slowly, while you change, slowly, beside it.

The pleasure is also the pleasure of not needing to look at the map. The pleasure of walking a trail so often that you can walk it with your eyes closed, which is not a thing you should do, but which is the kind of thing you can almost do, when you have been going to the same forest for years. The pleasure is the pleasure of stopping, on a particular corner, in a particular light, and saying, to no one in particular, here, this is the spot. The spot has no name. The spot is yours.

## the weekend, as a structure

There is something to be said, also, for the weekend. The weekend is, in our current arrangement, the only time we have, in any predictable way, for the slow practice of walking a known place. The weekend is also, of course, the time we have been told, by every lifestyle magazine, to fill with as much novelty and adventure as we can afford. We want to fill it with flights to a new city, with reservations at a new restaurant, with tickets to a new show. The weekend, we are told, is for living. The weekday is for surviving.

I want to argue, gently, against this. The weekend, I want to suggest, is also, and maybe more, for the slow, unglamorous, deeply ordinary practice of walking the same trail, in the same forest, in the same pair of shoes. The weekend, I want to suggest, is the only time most of us have to be in a place we actually know, instead of a place we have just arrived at. The weekend, I want to suggest, is the only time most of us have to be a person who lives in a particular place, instead of a person who is just passing through.

I do not, by this, mean to argue against novelty. There are places I have been once, in my life, that I will remember until I die. There are places I have been that I will go back to, when I can. There is, of course, a place for novelty, and adventure, and the strange pleasure of being a stranger in a strange city, none of which I want to argue against. I mean only that there is also a place, and this is the place I am interested in, for the slow repetition of the same trail, in the same forest, on most weekends, for a long time.

The slow repetition is, I think, the kind of thing we have lost. We have lost it because the world has told us, for many years, that slow repetition is the same as stagnation. The world has told us that the only thing worth doing, on a weekend, is the new thing. The world has, I think, been wrong about this, in the way that the world has been wrong about many things. The world has been wrong because the world has confused novelty with depth. Novelty is, by definition, shallow. Depth, by definition, requires repetition. You cannot know a place deeply in a single visit. You can only know a place deeply by visiting it, slowly, again and again, until the place has become part of you.

## the small details, accumulated

I have, on the trail near my house, a small catalogue of details. There is the tree, near the second stream crossing, that has a woodpecker's nest in it, which I check on every walk, in April, with the attentiveness of a nervous aunt. There is the rock, just past the third switchback, that has a thin stripe of quartz running through it, which catches the light, on certain mornings, in a way that has made me stop, more than once, and just look. There is the patch of trilliums, on the south-facing slope, that come out, every spring, slightly earlier than the year before, which I have come to interpret, without any evidence, as a sign of something I cannot quite name.

None of these details is, by itself, important. The woodpecker's nest is, in the larger scheme of things, just a hole in a tree. The quartz stripe is, in the larger scheme of things, just a piece of rock. The trilliums are, in the larger scheme of things, just a small white flower. None of them matters, in any way that the books, the apps, the lifestyle magazines would recognise as mattering. All of them matter, in the way that a place you know matters. All of them are the reason you go to the trail in the first place.

The small details accumulate. The accumulation is the point. The accumulation is what makes the trail yours, in a way that no single visit could. The accumulation is what makes the forest, not just a forest, but your forest, in the same way that a friend is not just a person, but your friend. The accumulation is what makes the weekend, not just a weekend, but a particular weekend, in a particular season, in a particular year of your life, which you will, for the rest of your life, remember as the weekend you saw, for the first time, the woodpecker come out of the hole.

## what the trail is for

The trail, in the end, is not for anything, exactly. The trail is not for fitness. The trail is not, mostly, for the view. The trail is not for the photograph. The trail is, mostly, for the practice. The practice is the slow repetition, the slow accumulation, the slow knowing of a place. The practice is, in the end, what the trail is for.

The trail is also, I think, for the weekend. The weekend is the only time, in most of our lives, when we can do a thing without justifying it. The weekday, we have to justify. The weekday has the meeting. The weekday has the deadline. The weekday has the school run. The weekend, briefly, does not have to justify anything. The weekend can be, if we let it, the time we give ourselves, in return, for the weekdays. The weekend is, in this sense, a small weekly gift, from us, to us.

I have come to think that the best way to spend this gift is to walk a known trail. Not a new trail. Not a trail that has been recommended by a podcast. A known trail. A trail you have walked, in your own shoes, in your own weather, in your own company, for many years. A trail that has, in the slow accumulation of small details, become part of your life. A trail you could walk with your eyes closed. A trail you have walked with your eyes open. A trail you will walk, if you are lucky, next Saturday, and the Saturday after, and the Saturday after that, until the trail has become, in some quiet way you cannot quite name, the spine of the week.

So choose a trail. A place you can walk to, on a Saturday, in less than an hour. A place that is not, in any objective sense, remarkable. A place that has, in the slow accumulation of small details, become yours. Walk it. Walk it again. Walk it until the trail has become the weekend, and the weekend has become the trail, and the small details have become the spine of a life you were not, when you started, quite sure you were building.

The trail will be there. The weekend will be there. The small details will accumulate. The rest will follow.

The White Shirt, and the Quiet Workhorse You Keep Reaching For
A white cotton shirt hanging in soft light
One good white shirt, washed a hundred times, soft at the collar and a little translucent in the back — the most loyal piece in the closet.

Somewhere in your closet, almost certainly, there is a white shirt. It may not be the most expensive thing you own. It is probably not the newest. But it is the thing you reach for when you do not know what to wear, when the morning is uncertain, when you need to feel, by ten a.m., that you have made at least one decision correctly. You reach for it. You put it on. And the day, somehow, becomes a little bit more possible.

This is the strange, almost invisible, work of the white shirt. It is the piece that, more than any other in the wardrobe, has learned how to disappear into its own usefulness. It does not announce itself. It does not ask to be admired. It simply shows up, day after day, and asks to be of service.

![A white cotton shirt draped softly over the back of a wooden chair beside a window](https://images.pexels.com/photos/4440566/pexels-photo-4440566.jpeg?auto=compress&cs=tinysrgb&dpr=2&h=650&w=940&w=1800)

## a history written in cotton

The white shirt has a longer biography than almost anything else in the modern wardrobe. It has been, at various points, a symbol of labor and a symbol of leisure, a uniform of service workers and a signature of the leisure class. It has been starched into armor by bankers and rolled into the carry-all of painters. It has crossed centuries and continents, and it has done so by remaining, in essence, unchanged.

What changed, mostly, was the cloth. The early versions were heavy and coarse, more linen than cotton, and they were worn more as an undergarment than as a statement. The version we know now — the one that hangs in your closet on a thin wooden hanger — is a relatively recent invention. It belongs, properly, to the twentieth century and to the slow democratization of what we now think of as office-appropriate dress. Somewhere between the rise of the white-collar worker and the arrival of the washing machine, the white shirt became, for most of us, the default setting of a public self.

This is, when you stop to think about it, an enormous cultural accomplishment for a piece of clothing that, at first glance, has no color and no ornament. The white shirt has managed to become meaningful precisely because it refuses to mean anything in particular. It is the blank page on which the rest of the outfit is allowed to write.

## the collar is the whole thing

If we were going to identify the single part of the white shirt that does the most work, we would not begin with the cotton or the buttons or the cut. We would begin with the collar. Because the collar, more than any other part of the shirt, is the thing the eye actually sees.

The collar frames the face. The collar carries the tie, if there is one. The collar touches the jaw, the place on the body where you carry your tension and your age. The collar is, in this sense, the most architectural feature of the shirt, the one that does the most with the least.

Which is why, when you have finally worn a white shirt down — when you have laundered it a hundred times and the collar is soft and the cotton has started to thin at the elbows — what you notice first is the collar. You notice the place where it has begun to relax, just slightly, around the neck. You notice the way it sits, less like armor now and more like a kind, familiar hand.

The collar is also where the shirt does most of its aging. The cuffs fray a little, certainly. The hem softens. The shoulders, almost imperceptibly, lose the line they once held. But the collar is where time chooses to make its argument. A shirt whose collar has begun to soften is a shirt you have worn enough to trust. It is the kind of shirt you stop having to think about.

### a small conspiracy of washing

There is also, hidden in the white shirt, a small conspiracy of laundering. The white shirt is, more than almost any other garment, defined by how it is washed. The bright, optic white of a brand-new shirt is a thing that cannot really be restored; it can only be preserved by a particular kind of attention. This is part of why the white shirt remains, even in an age of fast fashion, a relatively considered purchase. People do not, generally speaking, throw a white shirt away after three wears. They wash it carefully. They iron it, or they send it to be ironed. They keep it on the hanger, in the closet, with the spare button still sewn into the small flap on the inside of the placket.

This is a discipline that has largely disappeared from the rest of the wardrobe. Few of us, anymore, think of how we wash a sweater or a pair of trousers. But the white shirt has retained, almost by survival, a small etiquette. There is the hot water. There is the gentle detergent. There is the hanger, and the line-dry if you can bear it, and the iron with the steam setting low. The white shirt asks for these things, and the relationship between a person and a white shirt is, in part, defined by whether these small requests are honored.

When they are, the shirt repays you with years of useful life. When they are not, the shirt becomes, very quickly, the kind of off-white that is no longer quite the thing you hoped it would be.

The Window, and the Frame That Brings the Outside In
A large window with soft daylight pouring through
A room with a real window is never the same room in winter and summer — it is the cheapest artwork in the house.

There is a window in the apartment where I grew up that I have never been able to forget, even though it was, by any measure, an ordinary window. It was set into the wall above the kitchen sink, single-glazed, slightly fogged at the corners from years of condensation, and framed in white-painted wood that had yellowed the way all white-painted wood yellows if you do not repaint it often enough. It did not face anything particularly grand. It faced the side yard of the neighbor's house, a strip of lawn, a clothesline, and a wooden fence that leaned slightly to the left. There was nothing there to look at. And yet my mother, who washed a great many dishes in front of that window over the years, used to say that the window was the reason she did not mind doing the dishes. I understood, even as a child, that she was not really talking about the window. She was talking about the kind of attention a window makes possible — the kind of attention that turns an ordinary task into something you almost look forward to.

A room with a real window is never the same room in winter and summer. The same walls, the same floor, the same objects — and yet the room itself changes three or four times a day as the light moves across it, and changes again, more slowly, as the season turns. In January, the light arrives late and leaves early, and arrives already tired, slanting across the room at such a low angle that it draws long shadows of every object onto the wall behind it. In June, by contrast, the light is sudden and overhead, and the room at noon is almost too bright to inhabit, and the window becomes less a frame than a barrier — a place where the outside is held at a polite distance. We tend to think of the room as the fixed thing and the light as the variable. It is more accurate, I think, to say that the light is the room. The walls are only the container.

![A large window with soft daylight pouring through](https://images.pexels.com/photos/19026351/pexels-photo-19026351.jpeg?auto=compress&cs=tinysrgb&dpr=2&h=650&w=940&w=1800)

## What a Window Is Actually For

If you ask an architect what a window is for, the answer is almost always about daylight, ventilation, view, or a combination of the three. These are the legitimate reasons. They appear on floor plans and in building codes. They are the reasons a window passes inspection.

But if you ask a person who has lived for a long time in one room what the window is for, the answer tends to be stranger and more particular. The window is for watching the dogwood leaf out in spring. The window is for noticing, in October, that the maple across the street has begun to turn before any of the others. The window is for hearing, in the early morning, the sound of the milk truck two blocks away, and knowing from the sound alone what the weather is. The window is for the hour, usually late on a Sunday afternoon, when the cat finds a patch of sun on the sill and sits in it with the slow satisfaction of a creature who has, after many attempts, finally understood how windows work.

None of these are functions that show up on a floor plan. None of them are functions a developer would put in a brochure. And yet, if you took any of them away — if the window were replaced by a wall, or by a sheet of glass that could not be opened — the room would not be the same room. It would still be the same square footage. It would still contain the same furniture. But it would be a quieter, smaller, more self-enclosed place, and the lives lived in it would, over time, become correspondingly smaller too.

A window is not, in the end, an opening in a wall. It is a relationship with somewhere else. It is the room's continuing conversation with the rest of the world — with the weather, with the season, with the neighbor, with the bird on the sill, with the streetlight that comes on at dusk. A room without a window is a room that has nothing to say to anything outside it, and that is a lonelier thing than we tend to admit.

## The Frame, and What It Edits

Every window is also a frame, and frames, as anyone who has ever held a piece of paper up to a view knows, are not neutral. A frame decides what part of the world you are looking at. It decides the proportions, the aspect ratio, the size of the slice. It decides whether the view feels intimate or grand, panoramic or concentrated. The same view — the same backyard, the same trees, the same fence — can feel very different depending on whether the window is tall and narrow, like a porthole, or wide and low, like a landscape painting, or set high in the wall, like a clerestory, so that you see only sky.

This is why choosing a window, or choosing the curtains for one, is a more serious act than it looks. The curtains, in particular, are not decoration. They are the second frame. They are the frame you impose on the frame the architect imposed on the view. You can choose to leave the window uncurtained, in which case the view is naked and unmediated and changes every hour. You can choose to curtain it heavily, in which case the view becomes a thing you decide to look at, like turning the page of a book. You can choose a sheer curtain that turns the view into a watercolor, in which case the outside becomes atmosphere rather than image. None of these choices is wrong. Each is a different way of relating to the world on the other side of the glass.

I have come to prefer, over the years, the lightest possible touch — a linen panel that filters but does not hide, that lets the room remain in conversation with the outside even when the curtain is drawn. There is something about a heavily curtained window that makes me feel, even when the curtains are open, that the room has decided to retreat from the world. The room becomes a little more sealed, a little more self-sufficient, a little less interested in what is happening outside. For some people, at some moments, that is exactly right. We all need rooms that close themselves off. But for the rooms where we spend our ordinary hours — the rooms where we eat breakfast and read the paper and watch the light change — I want the thinnest possible membrane between inside and outside. I want the world to come in uninvited.

## Winter, and the Window That Earns Its Keep

In summer, a window is easy to love. The air moves through it. The light is generous. The view, whatever the view is, looks its best. In winter, by contrast, a window becomes something more like a difficult companion — one that lets the cold in, that sweats with condensation on cold mornings, that has to be defended against with weather-stripping and secondary glazing and the occasional towel pressed along the sill. In winter, you discover whether your windows were well made or not. You discover whether they were installed by someone who cared or by someone who was being paid by the unit.

But winter is also when you discover what the window is really for. In winter, the light is so scarce, and so low, and so particular, that every window becomes a kind of gift. The sun arrives at an angle it never reaches in summer, and it reaches into parts of the room that the summer sun, high overhead, never touches. A patch of floor that is unremarkable in June becomes, in February, the only warm place in the house. A wall that is invisible in summer becomes, in winter, a small screen onto which the bare branches of the street tree throw their shadows. You find yourself rearranging the furniture to follow the sun, the way the dachshund of a friend of mine rearranged himself every afternoon for fifteen years, sliding from one patch of light to the next as the sun moved across her living room, until one day he did not get up, and the light reached the spot anyway, and no one was there to receive it.

There is a melancholy in winter windows that I do not think we should try to design away. The condensation on the glass. The fact that you can sometimes see your own breath inside the room, briefly, when the temperature is right. The fact that, even with the curtains open, the view outside looks colder than the view you remember from August. All of this is the window doing its full work. It is reminding you, all winter, that the room is part of a larger world, and that the larger world is, at this moment, colder than the room. That small piece of news, delivered to you every morning without commentary, is, I think, one of the most underrated gifts of living in a house with real windows.

## The Window That Brings the Outside In

There is an idea, common in certain traditions of interior design, that the window is a problem to be solved. The view is too distracting — solve it with a frosted film. The light is too bright — solve it with blackout curtains. The street is too close — solve it with a hedge, or a fence, or a higher sill. The outside, in this view, is an intrusion. The window is a defect in the wall. The job of the designer is to minimize the defect.

You find yourself rearranging the furniture to follow the sun, the way the dachshund of a friend of mine rearranged himself every afternoon for fifteen years, sliding from one patch of light to the next as the sun moved across her living room, until one day he did not get up, and the light reached the spot anyway, and no one was there to receive it.

There is a melancholy in winter windows that I do not think we should try to design away. The condensation on the glass. The fact that you can sometimes see your own breath inside the room, briefly, when the temperature is right. The fact that, even with the curtains open, the view outside looks colder than the view you remember from August. All of this is the window doing its full work. It is reminding you, all winter, that the room is part of a larger world, and that the larger world is, at this moment, colder than the room. That small piece of news, delivered to you every morning without commentary, is, I think, one of the most underrated gifts of living in a house with real windows.

The Window That Brings the Outside In

There is an idea, common in certain traditions of interior design, that the window is a problem to be solved. The view is too distracting — solve it with a frosted film. The light is too bright — solve it with blackout curtains. The street is too close — solve it with a hedge, or a fence, or a higher sill. The outside, in this view, is an intrusion. The window is a defect in the wall. The job of the designer is to minimize the defect.

I have come to think this is the wrong way around. The outside is not an intrusion. The wall is an intrusion. The wall is the strange thing — the barrier we put up between ourselves and the rest of the world. The window is the apology we offer for the wall. It is the place where the wall admits that it is not, in the end, what the wall most wants to be. A room with too few windows feels, to me, like a room that has forgotten why it exists. It is a room that has retreated so far into itself that it has stopped being a room at all and has become, instead, a small fortress.

A room with a real window — a window that opens, that lets the light in at every hour, that frames some particular piece of the world, however humble — is a room that is still in conversation. It is a room that is still interested in the day. It is a room in which the weather, whatever the weather is, is allowed to arrive.

That, more than any sofa or any paint chip or any carefully chosen piece of art on the wall, is what a window is for. It is the cheapest artwork in the house, and the most constantly changing, and the one that no interior designer, however talented, can improve upon.

Wood, and the Patina It Carries, and the Small Beauty of a Surface That Has Actually Been Used
A close-up of an aged wooden surface showing grain and wear
A wooden table that has been used, spilled on, sanded, and used again is a record of every meal it has held.

If you run your hand across the surface of a wooden table that has been in use for fifty years, you can feel the entire history of the table under your palm. The grain is still there — that part does not change — but the surface is no longer flat. There are slight valleys where the soft grain has been compressed by years of elbows, plates, hot pans, water glasses, newspaper sections spread out for breakfast. There are ridges where the harder grain has held its line against everything that has been set on top of it. The table no longer has a single surface. It has many surfaces, layered, the way a piece of land has many surfaces once you begin to look at it closely.

This is what people mean, I think, when they speak of patina. They mean the way a material begins to record the life that has passed over it. Not damage, exactly — or not only damage. More like the slow accumulation of being useful. A wooden table that has been used, spilled on, sanded, and used again is not less beautiful than the day it was made. It is more beautiful, in a way that no photograph of the new table can quite capture, because the beauty it now holds is the beauty of having mattered.

![A close-up of an aged wooden surface showing grain and wear](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1776886393253-088586fc8859?crop=entropy&cs=tinysrgb&w=1800&q=82)

## Why We Want the Surface to Remember

I think the longing for patina is one of the deeper longings in domestic life, and we rarely admit it to ourselves. We say we want a wooden table because wooden tables are warm. We say we want a solid oak floor because oak is durable. We say we want a hand-thrown clay bowl because clay is honest. These are true reasons, but they are not the whole reason. The whole reason is that we want to be in a room that is changing in the same direction we are changing. We want to be surrounded by materials that age the way we age — slowly, unevenly, in ways that record what has happened to them.

A new piece of furniture is, in this sense, the saddest piece of furniture. It is a piece of furniture that has not yet been loved. It is a piece of furniture in its first costume, before any of the lives it will participate in have left their mark on it. We see it in the showroom and we feel a small flicker of tenderness for it — for the version of itself it is about to become — and we take it home, and we use it, and a year later we cannot remember why we ever found it cold.

The table that matters in a house is never the table that arrived last. It is the table that has been there through the most. It carries the silver scratches of the year the children first started helping in the kitchen. It carries the dark circle from the year the pipe leaked and someone set a pot under it. It carries the faint smell of lemon oil that belonged to the previous owner, twenty years ago, and has never quite faded. It is not a surface. It is an archive.

## On Forgiving and Unforgiving Materials

There is a distinction, in domestic materials, between those that forgive use and those that fight it. Wood is at the forgiving end of the spectrum, along with linen, leather, brass, wool, and unglazed clay. These materials are not destroyed by being touched. They are improved by being touched. They accept scratches as additions rather than subtractions. They age into themselves. They wear in, the way a pair of good shoes wears in.

At the other end of the spectrum are the unforgiving materials — polished granite, lacquered MDF, stainless steel with a mirror finish, anything that has been sealed under a layer of plastic or glass. These materials do not absorb use. They deflect it. The first coffee ring that lands on them stays, faintly, forever. The first knife scratch reveals a different color underneath. The first dent becomes a permanent accusation. The room made of these materials begins to feel, after a few years, like a room that is disappointed in the people who live in it.

You can see the difference immediately when you walk into a house. A house full of forgiving materials feels lived-in, in the good sense — settled, worn, warm under the hand. A house full of unforgiving materials feels staged, even when no one is trying to stage it. The surfaces have an edge to them. The light bounces off them with a kind of impatience. You feel that you have been admitted, temporarily, to a room that does not really want you there.

The cost difference, interestingly, is not always as large as we think. A solid oak table, bought once and used for forty years, costs less per year than the engineered-wood table that has to be replaced three times in the same span. A linen slipcover, washed and rewashed, will outlast three sets of synthetic upholstery. We have been taught to associate quality with shine, and shine with newness, but the materials that actually improve our daily lives are usually the ones that lose their shine first.

## The Table as a Slow Companion

A wooden table is a slow companion. It does not announce itself. It does not demand attention. It does not change week to week. But if you are paying attention, you can watch it change year to year. The darkening at the center where the afternoon sun reaches. The lightening along the edge where no one ever sits. The small crack that opened one winter when the heating was off for a week, and that has since closed again, but left a faint line. These are slow changes. They are the kind of changes that make a home feel inhabited rather than decorated.

There is a particular pleasure, on a quiet Sunday morning, in running a cloth over a wooden table and feeling, under the cloth, the grain. The grain is a kind of map. The softer parts feel slightly different under the cloth than the harder parts. You can trace a line with your fingertip and follow it across the table for almost a foot before it disappears into another line. No two tables have the same grain. No table has a grain that is meaningless. Every piece of wood is a record, frozen in cellulose, of how a tree once grew — which direction the prevailing wind came from in the year this ring was laid down, which years were wet and which were dry, which years the canopy above this branch was thin and which years it was crowded.

When we set a glass on top of all that, we are setting it on a piece of time. We are using a piece of forest as a side table. The gesture is so ordinary that we forget how remarkable it is. A two-hundred-year-old oak, still bearing the history of every year it lived, now bearing the coffee rings of every breakfast since. This is what we are asking of wood, when we bring it into our houses. We are asking it to carry us, too, the way the tree once carried the wind.

## Living with Imperfection, On Purpose

Choosing a wooden table, then, is also a choice about imperfection. We are choosing to live with a surface that will, over time, look less perfect than the day it arrived. We are choosing a surface that will record the mistakes — the hot pan set down without a trivet, the candle that dripped, the wine that was not wiped up quickly enough. The table will not be ruined by these events. It will absorb them. It will integrate them. But it will not be the same table it was.

Some people cannot tolerate this. They want their surfaces to remain as they were. They buy the lacquered versions, the sealed versions, the versions that promise, in their marketing, to remain pristine. These tables do remain pristine, for a while. And then, because life happens, they do not. The first scratch lands, and the table becomes a thing that has been ruined. It cannot be restored to its original state, because its original state was a sealed, finished state that was always going to end.

The wooden table, by contrast, can always be sanded. It can be re-oiled. It can, in extremis, be planed down by a handyman who knows what he is doing, and the new surface will go on accumulating its own patina from that point forward. The table does not have a single perfect state. It has a sequence of states, each one a little more marked than the last. There is no version of the table at which the patina is complete, because the table is still being used, and will be used tomorrow, and the day after that, for as long as the house stands.

This is, I think, what we are really choosing when we choose wood. Not a surface. A relationship. A relationship with a material that will change in our hands, that will carry our marks, that will become, in time, a kind of mirror of the years we have spent with it. We are choosing to live with something that is becoming itself, slowly, in the same room in which we are becoming ourselves.

That is a generous thing to ask of an object. Wood, fortunately, is generous enough to accept.
